West End legend Dame Elaine Paige has revealed she “lived on sleeping pills” for many years, revealing she kicked the habit during the pandemic.

The 78-year-old began her stage career in the 1960s and originated the role of Eva Perón in Lord Andrew Webber’s Evita in 1978, winning a Laurence Olivier award for best performance in a musical.

The role rocketed Paige into the spotlight and she collaborated with Lloyd Webber on a number of other occasions, also taking the lead as Grizabella in Cats and starring opposite Barbara Dickinson in Chess.

Speaking to The Sunday Times Magazine, Paige said in a new interview: “For many years in the theatre I lived on sleeping pills, otherwise you’re wired until 2am after a show.

open image in gallery Paige was awarded a damehood last year ( AFP/Getty )

“I called it my Judy Garland syndrome. They’re dreadful things to become addicted to, which I was. But since the pandemic I’ve managed to get off them and will not take one again.”

Paige continued: “I say to myself that even if I don’t sleep well, I’ll be fine the next day. I’m not ready to take afternoon naps yet.”

During her decades-spanning career, Paige has also released multiple albums and performed a number of concert tours, as well as appearing in television shows including BBC comedy Home From Home and the Alison Steadman-led drama Life. Since 2004, she has presented a weekly Radio 2 show, Elaine Paige on Sundays.

The singer was made a dame for services to music and charity in June 2025 and received a Special Award at the Oliviers back in April.

open image in gallery Evita rocketed Paige into the spotlight ( Getty )

The prestigious accolade was presented by Lloyd Webber, who read a letter from the Queen shortly before he handed Paige the prize at London’s Royal Albert Hall.

The message read: "I was delighted to learn you were to receive this year’s special award of the Oliviers 2026. I can think of no more fitting recipient."

Camilla further praised Paige’s "talent, commitment and generosity of spirit" which have made her a "truly defining figure in musical theatre”, adding, "you have quite simply brought huge joy to untold numbers of people across the globe, and we are all in your debt."

open image in gallery Paige with her Oliviers special award ( Ian West/PA Wire )

Accepting the award, Paige remarked: "Music and theatre have been the mainstay, really, well, the major force in my life and when I look back, I really can hardly believe the journey and the longevity of it all, to be honest."

She candidly recalled the early challenges of her career, including "bit-parts and chorus lines and lots of rejection and long stretches when the phone doesn’t ring".

Offering words of wisdom to emerging talent, Paige urged: "I wanted to say to the next generation, may you find your people, your voice and your courage and make sure to ignore anyone that says it can’t be done."

If you or someone you know is suffering from drug addiction, you can seek confidential help and support 24-7 from Frank, by calling 0300 123 6600, texting 82111, sending an email or visiting their website here.

In the US, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration can be reached at 1-800-662-HELP

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Liverpool and Arsenal get Barcola boost, Man City identify Rodri replacement
News.content:
Bradley Barcola was left out of Paris Saint-Germain’s squad for the French Super Cup in a boost to Liverpool and Arsenal’s chances of signing the France international winger. Barcola was also an unused substitute in PSG’s Super Cup win over Aston Villa on Wednesday. The European champions were set to demand £145m for the 23-year-old but Liverpool are prepared to play the long-game as they bid to negotiate a price as Andoni Iraola targets a new winger.

Elsewhere, Manchester City will sell Rodri to Barcelona in a deal worth up to £65m after finally accepting the advances of the Spanish champions. It means City will now accelerate their pursuit of Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old Moroccan wonderkid, as they enter talks to finalise a fee with Lille for the midfielder. And City could yet go back for Enzo Fernandez, despite missing Chelsea’s deadline for offers.

Arsenal are bidding to finalise their squad before the Premier League season, with Gabriel Martinelli and Ethan Nwaneri both left out of Sunday’s Community Shield. Both players have been linked with a move away and Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray on Friday. Arsenal have been keen to sign a defender following the injury to William Saliba and England defender Jarell Quansah, formerly of Liverpool, would be able to cover both centre-back and right back positions.

Wessex Water has become the latest water company to announce a hosepipe ban – its first in 50 years.

The firm, which supplies 1.4 million customers across Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire, last put a ban in place during the infamous hot summer of 1976.

The ban begins at one minute past midnight on Tuesday 18 August.

More than 27 million people across England are now under hosepipe bans.

It comes after the UK roasted in five heatwaves over the summer, with a potential sixth on the way before autumn arrives.

On Thursday, the hottest day of the year was recorded at London’s Kew Gardens, with temperatures reaching a sizzling 38.1C.

open image in gallery The UK experienced its hottest day of the year last week ( PA )

“After 50 years without a hosepipe ban in the Wessex Water region – the first since the famous drought of 1976 – this isn’t a decision we’ve made lightly and we’re sorry for the inconvenience it will cause,” Wessex Water chief executive Ruth Jefferson said.

“We know so many of our customers have already been taking steps to save water and we’re incredibly grateful for their support so far this summer. It makes such a difference.

“But the prolonged and extreme dry weather has meant demand across our region has consistently remained at more than 400 million litres per day, 30 per cent above average for this time of year and the equivalent of almost half a million hosepipes running for a full hour every day.

“While we’re not running out of water for essential use, our challenge has been moving water through the network quickly enough to meet these record levels of demand.

“This also has an impact on our underground storage reservoirs, which normally replenish with treated water quickly.”

open image in gallery The UK has roasted in five heatwaves so far this summer ( PA )

Wessex Water said that it is contacting larger business customers who are high water users to encourage them to avoid non-essential use.

It is also encouraging households to make small and simple changes during the ongoing dry spell to ensure water supplies and the environment are protected.

Those include letting the lawn go brown, using watering cans to water plants, keeping showers short and not washing the car.

A yellow heat health alert has been extended until 9am on Tuesday for the South East, South West, and London.

Rain and thunderstorms are expected for some this week, with showers becoming more widespread on Thursday.

“I can’t promise rain for all of us through the week ahead, but in the south at least, it’s looking like the most changeable week we’ve seen here – well at least since the end of June,” Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said.

The cycling community has rallied around the family of 19-year-old Finlay Tarling, who was killed in a collision at the Volta a Portugal, with the professional riders’ union “speechless and filled with anger” at his death as it called for a serious overhaul of racing safety measures.

The Welsh teenager was hit by a non-race vehicle on stage eight of the race last Friday and died shortly after the crash. The vehicle, which was driving the opposite way to the riders, was not prevented from getting onto the course despite the race having not entirely passed that section of road.

The Volta a Portugal, like many races below the level of grand tours including the Tour de France, does not fully close the roads for each stage but uses a rolling roadblock designed to protect the race convoy as it travels. Police and race organisation vehicles enforce temporary closures of certain sections until everyone involved in the race has passed through, before moving to the next section.

Carlos Catanario, of the National Republican Guard (GNR), told RTP that Tarling was off the back of the peloton and riding downhill to catch up, with the broom wagon - the final vehicle in the race convoy - behind him. Catanario said the driver involved in the collision had been waiting at the roadside for the race to pass and asked bystanders whether he could drive onto the road, then did so before the broom wagon had gone past, signifying the end of the rolling roadblock.

Catanario said the police escort “could not keep up” with Tarling and that there was no security presence preventing the non-race vehicle driver from accessing the course “because it was not one of the locations prioritised in the assessment that had been carried out”.

The incident is now subject to a police investigation, but Portuguese media have reported that the driver is unlikely to face charges.

Tarling’s death has led to calls for greater safety measures to be put in place to keep riders safe. The riders’ union, the Cyclistes Professionnels Associés (CPA), said: “We are speechless and filled with anger after the news of Finlay Tarling’s death at the Tour of Portugal. It is not right that a young athlete’s life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents.”

open image in gallery Finlay Tarling (second left) rode for the Great Britain Cycling Team and NSN Development ( Getty )

There has been a spate of deaths during bike races over the last few years. Swiss rider Gino Mader died aged 26 as a result of serious injuries sustained in a high-speed crash on a treacherous descent at his home race, the Tour de Suisse, in 2023. His compatriot, 18-year-old Muriel Furrer, died of traumatic brain injuries after crashing during the junior road race at the UCI World Championships - one of the sport’s most high-profile races - in Zurich the following year. She was not seen leaving the road and was not found for more than an hour. 19-year-old Italian cyclist Samuele Privitera died after crashing on a descent on the opening stage of the Giro della Valle d’Aosta last year.

The sport’s governing body, the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), has faced calls to implement stricter safety measures in response to what is widely felt to be an increasingly high-risk sport, with average speeds going up and racing increasingly conducted at ‘full gas’ pace from the start of every stage. This year’s Tour de France was the fastest on record, eclipsing the record set just 12 months prior. Additionally, the cost of race security has risen in recent years and race organisers are coming under increasing pressure after a series of high-profile incidents involving course security being breached.

open image in gallery Tarling won gold in the team pursuit at the British national championships in 2024 and was a talented time triallist ( PA Archive )

The last stage of the Tour Feminin International des Pyrenees was cancelled in 2023 after a series of near-misses involving riders and non-race vehicles driving on roads which were not closed to the public, with CPA president Adam Hansen saying the rolling roadblock was “not up to standard”. Several teams quit the men’s Etoile de Besseges race last year in protest at traffic entering the course and endangering riders.

Hansen has also called for changes to cycling helmets as a result of the increased speed of road racing. He told BBC Sport: “They need a major upgrade. Bike helmets only need to meet standard testing like all helmets. EU standard CE EN 1078 is only rated for 19.5km/h and I do not believe this is enough for road racing.”

The end of stage eight of the Volta a Portugal was neutralised and there was no stage winner as a result of Tarling’s death, while his team, NSN Development, withdrew from the race.

Many riders wore black armbands for the remainder of the race, while a minute’s silence was observed before the start of the ninth stage. Race leader Alexis Guerin wore a black jersey rather than the traditional leader’s yellow and Portuguese rider Rui Oliveira dedicated his win on stage 10, the final day of the race, to Tarling and his family, saying: “First I want to give my condolences to Fin's family, friends, team - everyone. It's been a rough couple of days. I can imagine what they're suffering.

“I said yesterday that I wanted to win for everyone that's supporting, but most of all for Fin's family and his team-mates. This one is for them."

Cambridge University’s chancellor has criticised the “racist feeding frenzy” that occurred in the two weeks before Professor Jason Arday’s death.

The 41-year-old, who became the prestigious university’s youngest black professor in 2023, had been the centre of media scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism in his work.

Prof Arday, who was found dead on Friday, resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education last week and an independent investigation into his appointment had been launched by Cambridge University.

The organisation Stand Up To Racism has announced plans for a vigil for Prof Arday to be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday.

On Saturday, prime minister Andy Burnham described the his death as a “tragedy on so many levels”, adding: “It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this.”

Speaking publicly for the first time, the university’s chancellor Lord Chris Smith said criticism of plagiarism could be investigated while questioning the way in which Prof Arday was treated.

open image in gallery Lord Chris Smith (pictured in 2025) has questioned the way Professor Arday was treated ( University of Cambridge )

In a statement, Lord Smith said: "I do believe it is possible to hold to two principles at the same time: to believe in the importance of academic integrity, and where criticisms of plagiarism arise, about any academic, whoever they are, ensure that they are rigorously investigated.

"And also to refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic. "

Before Prof Arday’s death, the university said it would investigate the circumstances around his “appointment and tenure”, and the findings would feed into a review of the process for appointing senior roles.

It is understood the university does not feel it is right to make a decision on whether to proceed with its investigation while the professor’s family are grieving.

A fundraiser for Prof Arday’s family, set up by Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, has raised more than £100,000.

Over 30,000 people have signed a Good Law Project petition seeking an inquiry into the recent coverage, accusing the media of “relentless harassment”.

Lord Simon Woolley, principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and a former mentor of Prof Arday, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House programme that his friend felt “hounded to death”.

open image in gallery Over 30,000 people have signed a petition calling for an inquiry into the ‘relentless harassment’ Professor Arday endured (Joe Giddens/PA) ( PA Wire )

Lord Woolley said: “In a conversation I had with Jason on the Monday – we met on Monday, with a few dear friends – he said he felt hounded to death, his words, that he couldn’t see a way out.”

He added: “On that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief.”

The crossbench peer said Prof Arday had been subjected to “the most horrendous, toxic, vicious witch hunt”, and called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.

“The whole of the black community and black academics have been brought into this debate as though we don’t belong in these positions, because we are collectively the diversity, equity and inclusion hires,” Lord Woolley added.

Prof Arday quit his role following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.

Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.

An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.

Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that his memoir book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on 27 August.

In a statement on Saturday, the publisher said: “Simon & Schuster is deeply saddened by the news of Jason Arday’s tragic death, and we send our condolences to his family during this devastating time.”

The boss of JP Morgan has warned the new chancellor against raising taxes on bank profits in the autumn Budget.

Reports suggest Jamie Dimon told John Healey in a phone call that higher taxes on the financial sector, while potentially popular with the public, could harm the government and its economic growth ambitions, as it could reduce investment, send jobs elsewhere and lower income for high earners who in turn spend in the wider economy.

Mr Dimon cited a decline in finance roles in New York that he partly blamed on the city’s tax burden, according to the Financial Times.

The paper cited a person briefed on the conversation saying Mr Dimon, one of the world’s most respected voices in the financial sector, warned against a windfall levy on bank profits or wider tax rises on wealth.

Mr Healey is reportedly due to have conversations with other bank executives in the coming days. At the end of July, the chancellor confirmed Wednesday 28 October as the date for his first Budget, after replacing Rachel Reeves.

And there have been repeated calls from within the UK’s financial sector to not allow rumour and speculation to damage business and consumer prospects in the run-up to this year’s fiscal event, as was the case last year.

Businesses held off spending due to uncertainty around incoming taxes, while some people withdrew money from their pensions early over fears that they would be subject to tax in future - which was ultimately not the case.

The influential chief executive of the US investment banking giant has previously sounded warnings against raising taxes on the industry and criticised the UK’s corporation tax surcharge for banks.

Some groups, including the Trades Union Congress (TUC), are calling for the Government to increase the windfall levy from the current rate of 3% to at least 8%, which it said would raise £9 billion for the Treasury over four years.

Earlier this month, Mr Dimon said in an interview for the Master Investor Podcast that he “always thought it was wrong”, adding: “JP Morgan did not damage the UK… I just thought it lacked principle to punish a company that had nothing to do with the crisis, and is still there 16-17 years later.”

Referring to the potential for the surcharge to be hiked, Mr Dimon said: “If the Government decides to do it then there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions to be made that they may not like.”

“If you have an uncompetitive tax system, capital leaves your country and… goes to other countries”, he warned, referring to an exodus of companies from London’s stock markets in the past two years.

“I wouldn’t want to see that, if I was running a country,” he said, stressing that he wants “to see the UK thrive”.

John Healey will deliver his first Budget as Chancellor on October 28 (Stefan Rousseau/PA)

Mr Healey will deliver his first Budget as Chancellor on October 28, following his appointment by Prime Minister Andy Burnham last month.

The former defence secretary is faced with the challenge of finding more money to fund Mr Burnham’s devolution priorities and increased defence spending, as well as new cost-of-living measures such as cutting VAT from energy bills and reducing business rates for pubs.

Experts, including the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr), have warned Mr Healey that he will need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Mr Healey has promised plans would be “built on fiscal discipline” and meet the fiscal rules set by previous chancellor Rachel Reeves.

News.title: ‘I get blanked as a woman in my own restaurant’: Tiella’s Dara Klein on sexism, toxic kitchen culture and Italian food
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. Sexism in the restaurant industry is a harsh reality Dara Klein knows all too well.

Despite founding one of London’s most-talked about new restaurants, Tiella Trattoria, on Columbia Road in January this year, she still battles ongoing gender bias.

The 36-year-old says she has encountered sexism not only from fellow chefs, but also from customers and suppliers.

“We have an open kitchen and the amount of times that I never get looked at in the eyes and blanked, even though I’m on the pass, reading out the tickets, running the ship, they’ll talk to the male chef on larder,” says the Italian chef, who recently published her debut cookbook La Trattoria.

Her experiences informed an open letter she co-authored with Sally Abe in February, condemning the “pervasive” sexism in the industry and calling for a more “inclusive, equitable and positive” environment.

Signed by a group of 70 female chefs, the letter, first published in The Telegraph in 2025, was written in response to Jason Atherton’s claims in a Times interview that he had not witnessed sexism in restaurants.

“The objective was always just to share an experience and it’s not done with blame and it’s not to finger point,” she says. “Unfortunately, I was always very, very aware of my gender [in kitchens] and I think a lot of women and non-binary people – and men too – have been made aware of that.

“When you’re working a physical, demanding and stressful job, it can all come to a standstill when somebody makes a comment just to remind you of the fact you’re a woman or talk about your appearance.”

It’s why now Klein’s main aim is to create a “warm and safe environment” for aspiring hospitality workers. More so than cooking, she hopes her legacy is to “inspire people to find this profession as it’s such a brilliant career in so many ways”.

open image in gallery ‘La Trattoria’, Klein’s debut cookbook draws on the regional Italian cooking that shapes the menu at Tiella ( Ebury )

Klein herself nearly didn’t become a chef. As a child, she “never, ever” had any desire to work in kitchens, even though it was the family business, and didn’t start cooking professionally until she was 28.

She grew up in San Giovanni in Italy’s Emilia-Romagna region before moving to Wellington, New Zealand at the age of six for her father’s work. Her mother, who’d worked in kitchens in Italy, was initially homesick and used cooking as a coping mechanism. It was then a business idea was born.

First, her parents opened a deli in the suburbs, before opening a restaurant, Maria Pia’s, with her mother as head chef. “She was definitely quite tough as a chef, so I always thought you had to rule with an iron fist. But the more I travelled, [the more] I saw there are different ways to run kitchens,” Klein says, adding that her mother comes from a “different generation of chefs”.

Initially wanting to pursue a career as an actor, director or screenwriter, Klein relocated to Australia to study creative writing and film, and later acting at Sydney’s prestigious drama school, The National Institute of Dramatic Art, but soon realised it wasn’t for her.

She then moved to New York to work a front-of-house position at a restaurant where she suffered a “mental health dip” and was advised by her family and doctors to switch to a nine-to-five office job for stability. For five years, she worked in various admin, marketing and social media jobs, but felt unfulfilled.

“I couldn’t really find my thing and, as somebody quite creative and busy, I found that really challenging. I was a bit lost and so I turned back to cooking,” Klein explains.

In 2019, she started working in kitchens in London before opening her much-lauded residency in The Compton Arms in Islington. After multiple offers of investment, she opened her first bricks-and-mortar restaurant, Tiella, earlier this year.

open image in gallery Klein says seeing different styles of leadership taught her that kitchens don’t need to be ruled with an ‘iron fist’ ( Caitlin Isola )

The restaurant focuses on rustic dishes from across Italy, such as chicken milanese, with a particular spotlight on the cuisine of Klein’s home region, Emilia-Romagna, which she says is famed for its “incredibly rich and decadent” cooking.

Klein remains a dedicated student of the different gastronomic traditions across Italy, highlighting Sardinia and Sicily as underrated food regions.

“Sardinia has a fascinating landscape as it’s pastoral but obviously it’s an island, so it’s enclosed with water. A lot of their pasta is fascinating , as well as the way they make cheese and produce their own salumi,” she says.

“There’s something about Sicilian food that really gets me as you see the influence of the various conquests from the Arab World and Northern Africa. They do different things with sweet and sour cooking and their approach to meat and fish is quite unique.”

But the one Italian dish Klein says overlooked by travellers is pizza rustica, a savoury pie, which is produced in the south, in places like Puglia, Calabria and Sicily.

“Our pies are really different and the one I love is made with a filling of tuna, onion, tomatoes, olives and red onion. They’re usually served at room temperature, so it’s something you’d bring to the beach,” she explains.

As for finding the best restaurants in Italy, Klein has some words of wisdom. “Stay off social media as the restaurants recommended there are more likely to be tourist traps,” she advises. “Go as far away from the centre of the city as you possibly can and spend time hitting the pavements, looking around at the restaurants.

“If the signage looks a bit old school, the clientele look Italian and it doesn’t look too flashy, that’s a dead giveaway. If the restaurant has fluorescent-strip lighting, often it’s going to be really good.”

Klein adds while laughing: “Definitely ask locals, but they’re probably not going to give you the good ones!”

Amatriciana (Rome): Roman tomato, guanciale and pecorino sauce

open image in gallery Klein’s amatriciana sticks closely to the Roman classic, with guanciale, tomato and pecorino ( Caitlin Isola )

“The first time I put amatriciana on the menu at Tiella I was incredibly nervous,” says Klein. “It’s one of the four great Roman pastas (along with cacio e pepe, gricia and carbonara) and since it’s my favourite of the lot, I wanted to honour the original recipe as much as possible.

“Speak to any Roman and they are deeply protective of their pasta, perhaps because so much of the world has taken their culinary ideas for a spin. There are times when I feel deeply passionate about tradition and ‘authenticity’, and others when I wish the rules would relax. When it comes to amatriciana, I wouldn’t dare mess with it.

“The dish is said to have originated in the town of Amatrice, neighbouring Rome. Supposedly the movement of shepherds between Abruzzo and Lazio brought the dish to the city. Gricia predated it, made with guanciale (cured pork cheek), pecorino and black pepper, but with the arrival of tomatoes in the 16th century, the dish evolved.”

Serves: 4

Ingredients:

150g guanciale

2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil

50ml white wine

1½ tins of plum tomatoes

1 fresh bay leaf

Pinch of red chilli flakes

120g freshly grated pecorino, plus extra for serving

Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper

Accompanying pasta shapes: spaghetti, rigatoni, paccheri, mezzi paccheri, bucatini

Pasta weight: 80-100g per person

Method:

1. Using a sharp knife, carefully trim the skin off the guanciale, trying not to remove any of the fat, then cut into thin strips.

2. Put the olive oil and guanciale in a heavy based pan and cook slowly over a low heat until golden and crisp. Remove a quarter of the guanciale and set aside.

3. Add the white wine to the pan and cook out the alcohol over a high heat for two minutes, then add the tomatoes, bay leaf, chilli flakes, a five-finger pinch of salt and a generous grind of black pepper. Simmer over a medium-low heat for around 20 minutes, stirring every five minutes or so. Taste the sauce for seasoning and adjust to your liking.

4. Cook your pasta according to the packet instructions, reducing the cooking time by one minute.

5. While the pasta is cooking, add the pecorino to the sauce and reduce the heat to low. Allow the cheese to melt into the sauce – do not stir or agitate it too much or it may clump.

6. Drain the pasta and immediately add it to the sauce along with a few tablespoons of the pasta water. Toss the pan back and forth to create the mantecatura (emulsification). Taste again for seasoning and adjust if necessary.

7. To serve, sprinkle with the crispy guanciale and some extra pecorino.

Risotto alla Milanese

open image in gallery Risotto alla Milanese gets its distinctive golden colour and delicate flavour from saffron ( Caitlin Isola )

“In many ways, this is the most iconic recipe in the canon of risotto,” says Klein. “The story goes that it was first cooked in the 16th century, created as a visual joke for the wedding of a master glassmaker’s daughter (saffron was used as a stained-glass colouring at the time).

“The first written documentation, however, appears around the early 19th century, with bone marrow and nutmeg among the ingredients listed. The dish was called risotto giallo until 1829, when the Milanese chef Felice Luraschi renamed it risotto alla Milanese.

“I like to allow the saffron to infuse very gently alongside a slowly melting ice cube. It may not be the fastest method, but I believe it extracts the flavour and colour beautifully.”

Serves: 4 as a primi

Ingredients:

4g saffron

1 onion

80g Parmigiano Reggiano

1.1 litres vegetable or chicken stock

125g salted butter

320g carnaroli rice

150ml white wine

Sea salt

Method:

1. Place a single ice cube in a small bowl with the saffron, allowing it to slowly melt at room temperature. Finely dice the onion and grate the Parmigiano. Pour the stock into a saucepan and warm over a low heat. Cube the butter and place it in the fridge. Weigh out the rest of the ingredients so that everything is ready to go.

2. Melt 25g of the butter in a wide saucepan over a medium heat. Add the diced onion and a five-finger pinch of salt and cook until soft and translucent. Add the rice, increase the heat to medium-high and toast in the pan for five minutes, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Do not skip this process. You’re looking for the rice to turn golden brown and release a toasted aroma. Add the wine and allow the alcohol to evaporate for one-to-two minutes.

3. Start a 20-minute timer and begin adding the stock one ladleful at a time, stirring constantly over a medium heat and waiting until most of the liquid has been absorbed by the rice before adding more. Do not give up on stirring – it’s worth it, I promise. Keep an eye on the timer and ensure you’ve used most of the stock by the end. Check for seasoning and the firmness of the rice every now and then. Don’t let the rice become soft and mushy: it should resemble al dente pasta.

4. Remove the risotto from the heat and add the remaining butter and the grated Parmigiano. Try to toss the pan, achieving mantecatura. The wave motion created by rocking back and forth will create an incredible emulsification, more so than just stirring, so give it a go. Stir in the saffron water (discarding any ice that hasn’t melted). Check the risotto for seasoning and add more salt if needed. I do not recommend adding black pepper as it will overpower the gentle flavour of the saffron.

5. Ladle generous amounts of risotto onto the plates and gently move it in a circle while tapping the bottom to achieve a nice flat layer. Serve immediately.

Panzanella: Bread and tomato salad

open image in gallery Tiella’s panzanella combines ripe tomatoes, stale bread, peppers, olives and basil in a classic Tuscan salad ( Caitlin Isola )

“Panzanella introduces us to the wide variety of Italian dishes created to use up stale bread,” says Klein. “It likely originated as a very simple bread and onion salad, evolving into the dish we know today after tomatoes were introduced to Italy from the Americas in the 16th century.

“The Renaissance poet Giovanni Boccaccio was one of the first to mention this Tuscan bread salad, calling it panmollo or ‘wet bread’, and the Florentine painter and poet Agnolo Bronzino described a version made with onions, cucumbers and purslane in one of his poems.

“This recipe is based on the panzanella at Tiella. It’s one of my favourite things to eat throughout the warmer months. I like to use stale sourdough or focaccia as they both hold up well against the marinade and don’t get too soggy.”

Serves: 4

Ingredients:

1 large pepper

200g slightly stale bread, preferably sourdough, ciabatta or focaccia

480g ripe tomatoes (I like to use a mix of varieties and sizes)

180g cucumber

65g red onion

60g black or purple olives

3 tbsp red wine vinegar (I used equal parts moscatel and Cabernet Sauvignon vinegar)

1 tbsp capers

1 tsp lemon juice

1 small bunch of basil

Extra virgin olive oil

Sea salt

Method:

1. Preheat the oven to 200C/180C fan/gas mark six.

2. Place the pepper on a baking tray lined with baking paper. Drizzle with olive oil and lightly season with salt, then roast in the oven for 40 minutes, turning halfway through. You want the skin to be slightly charred. Remove from the oven, transfer to a heatproof bowl and cover with cling film.

3. Meanwhile, make the croutons by cutting the bread into 3 x 4cm chunks. Season with a three-finger pinch of salt and drizzle over one tablespoon of olive oil. Massage the oil into the bread with your hands, then spread them out on a lined baking tray and bake in the oven for around 15 minutes, or until golden, rotating halfway through. Set aside to cool.

4. Wash and dry the tomatoes. Remove any stems, then cut into different-sized chunks. Place them in a large bowl and season with a five-finger pinch of salt. Wet your hands with cold water and flick a few drops of water on top of the tomatoes, then squish them down slightly with your hands. Leave them to sit for 15 minutes while you prep the other ingredients.

5. Wash and peel the cucumber. Cut in half lengthways, remove the seeds and then cut into thin slices on an angle. Finely slice the onion and soak in cold water to remove any sharpness. Destone the olives and tear them in half.

6. Once the pepper has cooled, remove the skin, stem and seeds, discarding any liquid released while cooling. Slice into thin strips.

7. Add the croutons to the tomatoes, making sure they soak up all the juices. You may need to add one-to-two tablespoons of cold water at this point if the croutons are looking too dry. Add three tablespoons of olive oil, the vinegar, olives, capers, lemon juice and a large pinch of salt. Drain the onions and add them to the bowl along with the sliced pepper. Toss the mixture together with your hands. Taste and add a little more salt, vinegar or lemon juice, if needed.

8. Once the salad is perfectly seasoned, stir through the basil leaves. Serve and enjoy immediately. This dish is great on its own or served alongside fresh mozzarella.

‘La Trattoria’ by Dara Klein (Ebury Press, £30).

News.title: AstraZeneca ditches lung cancer treatment trial
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. Drug giant AstraZeneca has revealed its latest setback in just over a month after halting a late stage lung cancer treatment trial.

The FTSE 100 firm said it found its Volrustomig drug, when combined with chemotherapy, was unlikely to boost survival rates for lung cancer patients when compared with another existing treatments.

Its move to stop the phase three trial follows a recommendation of the Independent Data Monitoring Committee after a planned review of data from the trials.

The decision marks a further blow after AstraZeneca saw billions wiped off its stock market value following its decision in July to stop a trial for a new heart disease drug, called Wainua.

Susan Galbraith, an executive vice president at AstraZeneca, said the decision to halt the lung cancer treatment trial was a disappointment.

She said: “While we are disappointed, we will learn from this trial and are determined to continue pioneering new medicines from our industry-leading pipeline in our quest to improve outcomes for patients with lung cancer.”

Lung cancer is the biggest cause of death by cancer, accounting for almost one in four (23%).

AstraZeneca said it would continue with trials for Volrustomig in treating other types of cancer, such as cervical cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and mesothelioma.

But the Anglo-Swedish group, which is headquartered in Cambridge, also revealed some oncology drug success on Monday with the announcement that its Enhertu treatment showed “a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival” for non-small cell lung cancer patients.

It will now continue into a phase three trial.

Ms Galbraith said: “This aggressive lung cancer often affects younger patients and has historically had limited first-line targeted treatment options, making these positive results an important step forward in bringing additional effective therapies to patients at metastatic diagnosis when there is the greatest opportunity to improve outcomes.”

And in another development, the group announced that results of its late stage trial of Tagrisso combined with Orpathys “reinforce Tagrisso as the backbone therapy” for a further type of lung cancer.

Shares in AstraZeneca lifted as much as 2% in Monday morning early trading.

Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG, said the Volrustomig trial setback was “another reminder of the risks facing the growth story”.

“While the underlying investment case remains supported by solid fundamentals and a robust late-stage pipeline, AstraZeneca needs positive clinical developments to rebuild confidence,” he added.

News.title: Rabies deaths are rising. What is going wrong?
News.content:
In a packed intensive care ward in Dhaka, three-year-old Abdul lay paralysed, his tiny body contorted by a rabies infection that had reached his brain.

His mother, Sheuli Akter, 38, sat at his side massaging his legs in the hope that this might loosen his muscles, but it was having no effect. Even his hands and feet were seized up by cramps.

Abdul had been in the hospital for a month but doctors said he was unlikely to live much longer. The infection, they said, had progressed to degenerative encephalitis; the virus had got to his brain.

Abdul was shaking, gripped by fever. His breathing was rapid and panicked, punctuated occasionally by groans of pain.

On his chin was the telltale scar of a dog bite, the source of the infection.

“He was playing outside with the other children,” said Sheuli. “The dog, which was one of those always waiting around outside, suddenly attacked him. They said it went for him because he was the smallest.”

News.title: Arsenal hunger is ominous for rivals as they dismantle Man City
News.content:
Was it the early goal that should have put Arsenal’s rivals on red alert? No. While Ricardo Calafiori’s intervention was dramatic, it wasn’t that. Was it the seamless introduction of the new signings, then? No, it wasn’t that either, despite the excellence of Bruno Guimarães and Christos Tzolis.

How about the emphatic scoreline – surely that was it? Again, the answer is no. Three unanswered goals against Manchester City will always grab a headline, but scorelines do not always define the nature of a performance or a team’s capabilities.

So what was it that should have those with pretensions of ripping Arsenal’s crown from their grasp shuffling uncomfortably? One word: hunger. The reason this was such an ominous afternoon for the chasing pack is the fact Mikel Arteta’s team played with intensity of a team with everything to prove.

Title wins can sometimes sate ambition. Players don’t always want to climb the same mountain again, not least if reaching the peak was initially so draining, but everywhere you looked on a day when Cardiff was painted red and white was evidence that Arsenal remain ravenous for success.

First Guimarães pounced out of the shadows to mug Jérémy Doku, leaving him in a heap. Then there was Gabriel Magalhães thundering into a befuddled Doku, celebrating in front of City’s fans as if he had scored, before Ben White flung himself in front of the Belgian, denying a clear-cut scoring opportunity.

News.title: Rashford returns and Fernandes misses another penalty as Man Utd humbled by Amorim
News.content:
Manchester United 2 AC Milan 4

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

News.title: Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season
News.content:
Newcastle United 1 Bayer Leverkusen 2

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

Sports.title: Awkward moment Arsenal star Piero Hincapie SNUBS handshake while collecting Community Shield medal as Zubimendi laughs
Sports.content:
PIERO HINCAPIE has gone viral for a brutal snub following Arsenal’s Community Shield triumph over Manchester City.

The Gunners laid down an early marker for the season on Sunday afternoon with a 3-0 win over Enzo Maresca‘s troops.



Hincapie came on for Riccardo Calafiori in the 60th minute of the Cardiff clash.

But it was his actions just before the trophy presentation which really got chins wagging.



After being presented with his winners’ medal, Hincapie accidentally snubbed a handshake offer from FA Chairwoman Debbie Hewitt.

The Ecuadorian appeared not to see Hewitt’s outstretched arm as he made his way to the podium.



His accidental snub of Hewitt left team-mate Martin Zubimendi in absolute stitches.

The Spaniard apologised for the defender’s faux pas and shook her hand before heading to the podium.

Footage of the incident went viral, with one of the Emirates faithful saying: “Hincapie is in a generational run right now.”

One remarked: “Hincapie was legit mesmerised by the medal lmao, doesn’t see the hand at all.”

Another chimed in: “Zubi is a total nice guy.”

Arsenal kick off their defence of the Premier League on Friday, welcoming newly-promoted Coventry City to the Emirates.

Sports.title: Unbelievable moment masked keeper produces RABONA clearance in cup clash as fans say ‘am I a few too many drinks in?’
Sports.content:
ABERDEEN fans were given a heart-in-your-mouth moment when their keeper bizarrely decided to make a clearance with a rabona.

German goalkeeper Marius Muller must have been pretty bored by the Scottish League Cup match against Dundee, which was goalless heading into the 38th minute.

So when his team-mate rolled the ball back to him in his own six-yard box, he decided to mix things up by completely unnecessarily making a rabona clearance.



He caught the ball pure and it flew all the way to the edge of the centre circle where his team-mate successfully got the first touch.



He was quickly dispossessed and a brief scrap over possession ended with the ball rolling again to Muller just seconds after his initial clearance.

But any fan fears were alleviated when he elected this time to flick the ball into his hands rather than try some other bizarre skill.

Aberdeen supporters were both enchanted and concerned by the mad moment.

One wrote: “Am I a few too many drinks in or has Muller done a 30 yard rabona?”

Another joked: “Love it, fantastic. Now don’t do that again.”

And a third added: “My head would be on mars seeing this if I was his manager.”

Indeed manager Stephen Robinson could only shake his head in disbelief when asked about the strange decision after the match, which Aberdeen went on to win 3-0.

Muller is already being talked about as a future cult figure with the Scottish outfit, despite only arriving last month – the rabona occurred in his sixth game for the club.

That status is probably helped by his unique look, sporting a face mask after suffering a number of head injuries during his career.

Sports.title: Serie A star rushed to hospital by helicopter and taken to intensive care after nearly drowning in pool
Sports.content:
SERIE A footballer Yael Trepy has been airlifted to hospital and put in intensive care after nearly drowning in a swimming pool.

The incident happened at a mansion in Sardinia, where Cagliari star Trepy, 20, was enjoying some downtime after a Coppa Italia win over Arezzo.



La Repubblica claim that Trepy is not a strong swimmer and ended up at the deep end of the pool, with L’Unione Sarda reporting that the youngster lost consciousness before being rushed to hospital.

Cagliari players were given two days off after Friday’s 1-0 victory, with Trepy playing 53 minutes before being subbed.



The club have updated fans with the following statement: “Yael Trepy is currently hospitalised at the Santissima Annunziata Civil Hospital in Sassari, where he is in intensive care.

“The Club is in constant contact with the healthcare facility and the player’s family and is closely monitoring the progress of his condition.

“At this time, Cagliari Calcio’s thoughts are with Yael and his family.

“The Club also requests the utmost respect for their privacy and will provide any updates when available.”

Trepy was born in France and learned his trade in the academy of Parisian club US Creteil-Lusitanos.



Cagliari snapped him up in 2022, and he scored against AC Milan‘s starlets to help them win the equivalent of the FA Youth Cup in 2025.

Trepy made his senior breakthrough last season, scoring once in eight Serie A appearances.

The Rossoblu, who finished 14th last term, get their league campaign underway at Parma on Saturday.

Sports.title: Barcelona fans give immediate Anthony Gordon verdict as £69m England ace makes first appearance since replacing Rashford
Sports.content:
BARCELONA fans came away excited after watching Anthony Gordon in their colours for the first time.

The England winger had his maiden outing for his new club over the weekend following his blockbuster £69million move from Newcastle.



Gordon, 25, lined up on the left as Barca took on Swiss side FC Basel at St. Jakob-Park.

The former Toon star was part of an attacking unit also including Fermin Lopez, Raphinha and fellow new recruit Karim Adeyemi.



And there were moments of promise as he ran at his full-back down the flank.

Commenting on Gordon’s performance, one Barca fan wrote on X: “We hope he keeps up this performance and continues to deliver like this”.

And a second gushed: “Trust me… Gordon will be the reason we win 2 UCLs before the end of this decade.”

A third swooned: “Could have easily gotten two goals from his play. He is direct and fits in perfectly with the sort of energy Flick wants, the depth, the varying attacking options we now have.”

Another added: “His low crosses are actually lethal man”.

Gordon got 45 minutes under his belt before being replaced by teenager Hamza Abdelkarim.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

The ex-Everton ace has replaced international team-mate Marcus Rashford at Barca.

Rashford, 28, scored eight goals in 32 LaLiga appearances on loan last season but has now returned to Manchester United – making his first Red Devils appearance in 611 days during Saturday’s 4-2 defeat to AC Milan.

Gordon was substituted yesterday with Barca level at 1-1 in Switzerland.

Adeyemi fired Hansi Flick‘s men into the lead, only for 17-year-old Jean Doucoure to equalise on the stroke of half-time.



Abdelkarim restored Barca’s lead shortly after the break, with Lamine Lamal’s penalty later making it 3-1.

Kazeem Olaigbe pulled one back from the spot, before Jesse Bisiwu’s late double added gloss to Barca’s win.

Barcelona will play their final pre-season friendly on Wednesday as they take on Egyptian side Al Ahly.

Flick’s men then begin their LaLiga campaign at Elche on Sunday.

Sports.title: Adorable reason why Cristiano Ronaldo married Georgina Rodriguez on August 11 with date holding very special meaning
Sports.content:
CRISTIANO RONALDO married Georgina Rodriguez on August 11 to mark a very important anniversary.

Ronaldo, 41, and Georgina, 32, finally tied the knot after a ten-year relationship that saw them getting engaged in 2025.



According to Vogue, the couple’s wedding took place six days ago on a symbolic date that marked a decade since the day they first met.

The Al-Nassr captain and the content creator met at a Gucci store in Madrid where she worked while he played for Real Madrid.



The pair got hitched in a private and intimate civil ceremony in Cascais, Portugal.

They became husband and wife in a romantic ceremony that took place in their living room.



Their five children – two of whom are biologically Georgina’s – were all in attendance.

That included Cristiano Jr, 16, twins Eva Maria and Mateo, both 9, who were born via surrogacy.

They were joined by Alana Martina, 8, and Bella Esmeralda, 4, who are mothered by Georgina.

The wedding also saw her sister Ivana, Ronaldo’s long-time friend Miguel Paixao and a Spanish couple named as Jose Rodriguez Sangil and his wife Monica Goncalez Martinez attending as the only witnesses.



The Manchester United legend’s mother Dolores Aveiro and his three siblings Hugo, Elma and Katia were not present on Tuesday.

This comes as Ronaldo confirmed this is likely to be the final season of his glittering 24-year career.

And the Portuguese captain added that he has his life post-retirement “all mapped out”.

Sports.title: Emi Martinez’s Juventus transfer collapses despite Aston Villa signing £30million replacement for Argentine
Sports.content:
JUVENTUS’ move for Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has fallen apart despite the Premier League club already lining up his replacement.

The Argentine goalkeeper and former World Cup winner has been heavily linked with an exit for the past two summers.



Italian giants Juventus finally seemed set to give him a new home after approaching Villa with a number of bids for the 33-year-old’s services this window.

But now, The Athletic have reported that the Bianconeri have decided to move on and pursue other targets after failing to agree a deal for the stopper.



That leaves Martinez in an awkward spot, with Villa already having a deal in place for his replacement Zion Suzuki.

The Japanese World Cup star seemed set to join French champions Paris Saint-Germain earlier this window.

But Villa pounced after that deal fell through late on, agreeing a deal with Parma that could be worth up to £30million.

He is set to arrive on a five-year contract.

The 23-year-old is understood to be the club’s first-choice for the upcoming season regardless of Martinez’s transfer status.

But with Villa set to compete in the Champions League this season, squad depth is on the agenda, and the two-time Yashin award winner would likely get some opportunity to play if he ended up as back-up this season.

Sports.title: Neymar’s bitter rival refuses to shake his hand as feud rages on SIX YEARS after pair first clashed
Sports.content:
FOE REAL Neymar’s bitter rival refuses to shake his hand as feud rages on SIX YEARS after pair first clashed

NEYMAR renewed his heated feud with Thiago Mendes as his bitter rival REFUSED to shake his hand.

Santos superstar Neymar returned to action in the Brazilian Serie A after retiring from Brazil following his last World Cup in July.



The star forward led his team on Sunday when they visited Vasco at Sao Januario in the league when tensions grew between him and Mendes, 34.

During the pre-match handshakes, the Barcelona legend greeted everyone but was ultimately snubbed by his rival – SIX YEARS after their beef first started.



Mendes didn’t accept a handshake from the 34-year-old, who was left smiling awkwardly before proceeding to greet the referees.

Their feud dates back in 2020 when Neymar played for Paris Saint-Germain.



Everything began during a Ligue 1 match when Mendes – then at Lyon – injured his fellow Brazilian.

The midfielder committed a late challenge that led to Neymar being carried off on a stretcher in tears.

Mendes was sent off after a VAR review and later received a three-match ban.

Neymar was diagnosed with a sprained ankle and was sidelined for about a month.



The Brazil legend’s father Neymar Santos Sr took to social media where he put Mendes on full blast.

The defensive midfielder, who apologised online, then claimed he and his family received threats and abuse following the incident.



Their rivalry was rekindled six years later this past February during Santos‘ 2-1 win at Vila Belmiro.

Neymar was enraged after a foul committed against him and confronted Mendes in the first half.

Shortly afterward, the pair began arguing until the ex-PSG star fell to the ground after the Vasco ace touched his face.

Both were shown yellow cards and kept arguing throughout the heated match that then saw Neymar bringing up the foul that led to his injury in France.

He said: “He always wants to start trouble, he always wants to act tough, it’s always like that.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“With all due respect, he’s an idiot. He already hurt me once at PSG, he threatened me today, so let’s see if he’s man enough to hurt me again.”

Neymar had the last laugh yesterday as he led Santos to a 3-0 victory against his bitter rival.

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim 'feels nothing' for Man Utd after perfect reunion following horror stint
Sports.content:
Ruben Amorim 'feels nothing' for Man Utd after perfect reunion following horror stint

Ruben Amorim insists his emotional attachment to Manchester United has gone after his AC Milan side got the better of the Premier League team in pre-season

View 2 Images Ruben Amorim got one over on his former side as AC Milan beat Man Utd

Ruben Amorim insists he "feels nothing for Manchester United" after getting the better of his former club in a pre-season clash at the weekend.

‌



The Portuguese coach was axed by the Red Devils in January but hired by AC Milan this summer - and the pre-season schedule saw the two sides meet in Poland at the weekend. Milan would secure a 4-2 win as Amorim got one over on his former team.

‌



The Italians had struggled in pre-season, losing 3-0 to Chelsea recently as Amorim found it difficult to have the impact he'd hoped for, but he landed a much needed win against the Premier League giants.

‌



Despite the build-up Amorim insists there was no added emotion when it came to facing United, where his tenure ended with him winning just 24 of his 63 matches, as the ex-Sporting Lisbon boss insists he feels nothing for them despite his previous connection.

Amorim told Sky Sport Italia: "No. For me, it was just a normal match. Since I signed with Milan, I've felt nothing about Manchester United. I'm just proud to have been at Man United and I still love the club, but after signing with Milan, I [feel] nothing bad about anything because I'm very happy, because I'm in the place where I want to be. I just want to continue here.

‌



"Of course, it was special to play against them again, but I wanted to win a game this preseason to present ourselves well in our league, to give a good image to our fans, so they can support us in our first match."

Amorim was appointed in November 2024 and would go on to preside over the club's worst ever Premier League finish, ending in 15th during a season that saw them win just 11 times. He would also lose in the Europa League final before his dismissal the following year.

View 2 Images Ruben Amorim endured a nightmare spell in Manchester (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

‌



Despite his Manchester struggles Amorim still landed the top job at one of Europe's most decorated sides and apologised to United upon his unveiling.

"It is hard to explain the mistakes as I would have to explain all the context of the last adventure," he said. "The only thing I can say is that I learn a lot and I did some mistakes.

"I didn't have [the] opportunity - and I am sorry for that - to say something to the Manchester United fans at the moment [but] I am really proud to have been their coach for a year."

Luis Enrique left both Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye out of his squad for Paris Saint-Germain's clash with Lens on Sunday amid strong interest from Liverpool

View 2 Images Luis Enrique shrugged off the question post-match (Image: Ligue 1)

Paris Saint-Germain boss Luis Enrique wasn't in the mood to discuss the futures of Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye after leaving the pair out of his squad to face Lens on Sunday. PSG missed the chance to win a second trophy in five days, as they were beaten 1-0 by Lens in the Trophee des Champions.

‌



Barcola, who's valued at an eye-watering £145million, and Mbaye, valued at around £40m, watched from the stands at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis amid strong interest from Liverpool. The Reds are keen to sign both wingers in separate deals.

‌



PSG have this week brought in Ferran Torres and Mika Godts to strengthen their forward line, pushing Barcola and Mbaye down the pecking order. But even with their two new signings not ready to face Lens, Barcola and Mbaye weren't invovled either.

‌



In his post-match press conference, Enrique was asked about the decision and gave a short shrift. "Thank you, goodbye," the PSG manager replied before walking out of the media room.

Kyllian Antonio saw red after a late studs-up challenge on Maghnes Akliouche, another forward who PSG recently signed. The hosts were forced to play with 10 men from the 39th minute onwards but held firm until the teams were balanced out.

View 5 Images Inter Milan want to sign the injured Curtis Jones (Image: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

2. Gakpo sends timely reminder

Another player who's been linked with an exit is Gakpo. Tottenham are understood to be pushing to sign the Netherlands international, with reports claiming that personal terms have already been agreed.

But Gakpo has remained professional and finished off a flowing move to break the deadlock on 23 minutes. Jeremie Frimpong drove inside from right-back and lifted the ball over Como's defence.

‌



Gakpo controlled it well and slotted home in one motion, sending a reminder to the Reds of what they'd be losing if they sell him to Tottenham. With Mo Salah gone, can Liverpool afford to lose another established forward?

View 5 Images Cody Gakpo is a target for Tottenham (Image: Darren Staples/AFP via Getty Images)

3. Jacquet's good first impression

With half-time looming, Como looked the more likely to score after a decent spell. But it was Liverpool who ended up doubling their lead before the interval.

‌



Jacquet - making his first appearance of pre-season after recovering from a knee injury - was the scorer, given a simple tap-in from Gakpo's low cross. It was a gift for the centre-back, who's had to be patient to get his chance.

There was more to Jacquet's performance than his goal, though. The former Rennes prospect was enjoying himself defensively; showing composure on the ball, putting in challenges and made a goal-saving tackle shortly before his strike.

Jacquet was replaced at half-time, as Araujo made his Anfield bow. Lewis Koumas - who'd played 25 minutes in the earlier game - was also introduced, coming on for Rio Ngumoha.

‌



View 5 Images Jeremy Jacquet scored a goal - and prevented one (Image: Darren Staples/AFP via Getty Images)

4. The Wirtz conundrum

When Liverpool shelled out a then-club-record £116million to sign Florian Wirtz a year ago, it was expected that he'd be rocking and rolling by now. But something still hasn't clicked.

The ex-Bayer Leverkusen star showed plenty of neat touches but didn't cause Como enough problems with his passing or dribbling. Fans are starting to doubt whether Wirtz deserves a starting berth, especially with Mac Allister on the verge of a return.

‌



Given time, one would expect his partnership with Alexander Isak to bear fruit. For now, though, perhaps pushing Dominik Szoboszlai further forward is a right call.

View 5 Images Florian Wirtz is a concern for Andoni Iraola (Image: Liverpool FC/Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

5. Next stop: St James' Park

So that's that. Liverpool's 2026 pre-season campaign is complete. The Reds have come away with three wins, two defeats and one draw from their six friendlies.

‌



Now the focus is on facing Newcastle, who've had a summer of change of their own. Iraola has a few selection headaches before next Sunday's visit to Tyneside, but could he have Bradley Barcola at his disposal?

Liverpool's top target remains at Paris Saint-Germain player and is valued at £145m. But with the transfer window closing in just over two weeks, PSG could be tempted to budge.

Sports.title: Man Utd ready to change tack in transfer market to match Chelsea and Man City
Sports.content:
Man Utd ready to change tack in transfer market to match Chelsea and Man City

Manchester United's record when it comes to selling players has left a lot of be desired in recent years, but Old Trafford chiefs hope to drive up sales with their new strategy

View 3 Images Radek Vitek recently left Manchester United (Image: Chris Vaughan/Getty Images)

Manchester United are attempting to monetise their academy in a bid to match their Premier League rivals. The Red Devils are putting a greater emphasis on young talent, not only with a view to strengthen their first-team but also improve the club's finances.

‌



It's a strategy that has already seen highly rated goalkeeper Radek Vitek leave on a permanent basis, despite an impressive loan spell with Bristol City last season and United's lack of depth in the goalkeeping department. Vitek, 22, was sold to Middlesbrough in a deal rising to £14million, with United inserting a 35 per cent sell-on clause plus a buy back option.

‌



The Mail report that United acknowledge the view that their historic conveyor belt has slowed over the past few years, while the likes of Manchester City and Chelsea have made millions from their academy products. It's added that 19-year-old left-back Harry Amass could be sold for roughly £7m plus add-ons before deadline day on September 1.

‌



Meanwhile, 22-year-old midfielder Toby Collyer is understood to be available. Fans may question the idea of offloading youngsters ahead of a season in which Michael Carrick's side will play at least 48 matches, having qualified for the Champions League.

"It's really important," Devaney, who captained United's under-21 side last term before a half-season loan spell in Scotland with St Mirren, said. "We speak about it as a group.

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher tells Man City to call off transfer immediately after Arsenal drubbing
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher tells Man City to call off transfer immediately after Arsenal drubbing

Arsenal dominated Manchester City as they beat Enzo Maresca's side 3-0 in the Community Shield at the Principality Stadium on Sunday afternoon

View 2 Images Jamie Carragher sent a transfer message to Manchester City during their Community Shield defeat to Arsenal (Image: (James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images))

Jamie Carragher has told Manchester City they must keep Rodri after watching Arsenal run riot in the Community Shield. The Gunners set a marker for the new season with a comfortable 3-0 victory over Enzo Maresca’s side in Cardiff.

‌



But new City boss Maresca omitted Rodri and Savinho as transfer speculation continues to surround them. Even though City have stated they want Rodri to stay and sign a new deal, it has become clear that he wants to leave, with Barcelona his preferred destination.

‌



The Catalan giants stepped up their interest in the midfielder earlier this week by making a second bid worth more than £51million. But as previously reported, City are asking for at least £70m for the World Cup winner.

‌



But as Carragher watched Maresca’s side come up short against the Premier League champions, the former Liverpool defender made clear he thinks that City need to cancel any talks to let Rodri leave. Taking to X, he wrote: “Arsenal 3-0. Man City have to keep Rodri.”

However, shortly after Carragher's post, Fabrizio Romano claimed that the Spaniard is closing in on a move to Barcelona after City 'gave the green light' to their latest offer.

On Sunday, Riccardo Calafiori opened the scoring after just 24 seconds for the Gunners before Kai Havertz added a second with a close-range header. Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard then wrapped up the win with a clever finish just three minutes after the break.

‌

Rodri has entered the final 12 months of his City deal, and speaking in his pre-Arsenal press conference, Maresca updated on the Spaniard’s future, saying 'anything can happen' as long as the transfer window is open.

‌



And speaking after his side’s defeat at the Principality Stadium, the new City boss said: "I think the goal we conceded after 25 seconds unfortunately affected the game in that moment.

View 2 Images Man City were well beaten as Arsenal lifted the Community Shield (Image: The FA via Getty Images)

“I think after the goal, the reaction was quite good before they scored the second one, we had three or four chances to score and draw the game but unfortunately we conceded the second one and it became more complicated."

‌



He added: "We have many things to work [on]. The season's just started so there are many things we need to do better but even when we win games there are things we need to do better."

Sports.title: Martin Odegaard puts Arsenal rivals on notice after Man City win - 'We want to win everything'
Sports.content:
Martin Odegaard puts Arsenal rivals on notice after Man City win - 'We want to win everything'

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard inspired his team to a fine 3-0 win over Manchester City to clinch the Community Shield - and then immediately set his sights on more silverware

View 2 Images Martin Odegaard insists Arsenal are coming for more silverware this season (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Martin Odegaard helped Arsenal humiliate Manchester City - before warning his rivals Mikel Arteta's men are on a mission to win everything this season.

‌



Arsenal swept City aside 3-0 to win the Community Shield in Cardiff, thanks to goals from Riccardo Califiori, Kai Havertz and Odegaard - his first in 2026. And Odegaard told the rest of the Premier League how champions Arsenal have the hunger for as many trophies as possible.

‌



Odegaard said: "We played some brilliant football. We showed our level. We showed we're ready, serious and want to do it again.

‌



"We want to attack it. When you get a taste of how nice it is, you want to do it again. We want to win everything."

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Arteta has now won two trophies in the last four months and he said: "I'm extremely happy with the performance. We talked about the desire we have - and to show how much we want it.

‌



"It's down to the preparation. I'm very impressed in the manner we played and competed.

"There is more belief. How to do it (win the title), and what it means. It makes a difference. I want to live those moments again. But we know it's going to demand something special."

This was Enzo Maresca's worst possible start to his mission of replacing Pep Guardiola. It was also his joint heaviest defeat as a manager in England.

‌



View 2 Images Odegaard and Kai Havertz celebrate Arsenal's killer third goal (Image: David Price/Arsenal FC)

He said: "The big part of the game was the first goal we conceded. Then the second one made it more difficult.

"I'm always concerned, even when we win games. We have a lot of things we need to do better.

‌



"We will re-set, analyse the game and start thinking about the next one. We can find many things after this kind of defeat. We were not switched on."

Captain Ruben Dias insisted there was a lot of work for his side to do. He said: "It's obviously not good enough. It is a final that we all wanted to win.

"If there is a lesson to be learnt in the final, let it be this one. You need to push through and make things work between us.

Article continues below

"We need to keep on working. and there's going to be lots of challenges along the way."
