What the US$3 Billion Actually Measures

Argentina runs dozens of trust funds, known locally as fondos fiduciarios. Each is a pot of money fed by a specific tax and reserved by law for one job.

One pays to patch highways. Another subsidises household gas bills.

The US$3 billion is what those funds had left over across 2024 and 2025. It is what they collected minus what they actually spent on their legal purpose.

The 2024 leftover was ARS 1.86 trillion (about US$1.98 billion at that year’s average rate). The 2025 leftover was ARS 1.23 trillion (about US$973 million).

Add them and you get roughly US$2.95 billion, rounded by the press to about US$3 billion. Each year was converted at its own official rate, not today’s.

This is not the whole public-works budget, and it is not a court finding. It is also not all of Argentina’s capital spending.

Capital spending is the money a state puts into new roads, dams and buildings. The trust funds are only one channel for it.

Who Counted It

The trail starts with La Nacion reporter Hugo Alconada Mon. He obtained the road fund’s accounts in early August and found most of the cash unspent.

LMDiario put the US$3 billion headline on it on August 16, citing official spreadsheets. Clarin ran the same figure that day, sourced to the Instituto Consenso Federal.

That institute is run by former congressman Alejandro “Topo” Rodriguez, a Peronist opponent of the government. So the headline number is an opposition reading of official data.

No Treasury table breaks the sum down fund by fund. Across all the trusts, 55.8% of the money collected was spent in 2024, and 69.5% in 2025.

The Road Fund at the Centre

The clearest case is SISVIAL, the national road fund created by decree in 2001. It lives off a slice of the tax on liquid fuels.

Between December 2023 and May 2026 it collected ARS 1.503 trillion (about US$1.01 billion). It spent ARS 394,406 million (about US$265 million) on actual road works.

That is 26.2% of the intake. Spending ran at 11.3% in 2024, 39% in 2025 and 18.5% in the first five months of 2026.

On May 31 the fund held ARS 1.001 trillion (about US$673 million) in financial investments. More than 85% of that sat in government bonds such as Boncap and Lecap.

Another ARS 37,761 million (about US$25 million) lay idle in a current account. Because the holdings are mostly Treasury paper, the road fund is in effect lending to the Treasury.

The water works fund tells the same story. On April 6 it held ARS 258,000 million (about US$173 million) in short-term Treasury notes — 88% of its assets.

Caputo’s Answer, and the Fiscal Record

Economy Minister Luis Caputo calls the whole thing “una operacion” — a political smear. He spoke in Cordoba on August 12.

He said: “That was already voted in Congress, it is in the budget, and we are on the way to delivering it.”

About 40% of the infrastructure money has been spent, Caputo added. He expects that to reach roughly 70% within two months.

No governor has complained to him, the minister says. A working group with governors and transport officials picks which projects get built.

Presidential spokesman Adrian Ravier was blunter. He could not say how much fuel-tax money reaches road maintenance.

Part of it, Ravier said, is directed by the Economy Ministry to help achieve fiscal balance. “Of course the law is being complied with,” he added.

That is the zero-deficit rule in practice — the promise that the state will not spend more than it takes in. Roads, Ravier argued, should increasingly be paid for by private investors.

The surplus itself is real. In July alone Argentina posted a primary surplus of ARS 4.79 trillion (about US$3.22 billion).

A primary surplus is what is left over before paying interest on the debt. After interest, July still ended ARS 4.47 trillion (about US$3.00 billion) ahead.

For January to July the primary surplus reached ARS 13.46 trillion (about US$9.04 billion), up 4.1% on the year. After interest it was ARS 3.81 trillion (about US$2.56 billion), down 26.8%.

Here is the awkward comparison. The US$3 billion built up in the trusts over two years is roughly the size of that whole seven-month bottom line.

The periods do not match, so it is not a like-for-like swap. It does show how much of the cushion comes from money that was not spent.

What the Complaint Does and Does Not Prove

On August 10 opposition congresswoman Victoria Tolosa Paz filed a criminal complaint in Buenos Aires federal court. It names Caputo, ministry and roads-agency officials, and Banco de la Nacion as trustee.

She alleges misuse of public funds. Tax money with “a specific and irrevocable destination” was “placed massively in financial instruments”, her filing says.

The complaint is days old. There is no case number, no named judge, no charges and no court finding.

Filing a complaint in Argentina is easy and settles nothing. Keep the two claims apart.

That the money was collected and not spent on roads is documented, and the government does not deny it. That it was illegally diverted is an untested allegation.

Opposition senators want to summon Caputo and Chief of Staff Diego Santilli. Decree 215/2024 handed the Economy Ministry control of every trust fund holding state money.

Why This Matters for Investors and Provinces

Argentina’s bond story rests on whether the surplus lasts. A surplus built partly on not building is easier to reverse than one built on permanent savings.

Deferred maintenance is a bill, not a saving. Potholed highways raise freight costs for grain, mining and energy — the exports foreign money is buying.

Provinces feel it first, and governors control votes in Congress. Milei needs those votes to keep his programme alive.

There is one more wrinkle for bondholders. When earmarked funds buy Treasury paper, the state is partly financing itself with its own reserved cash.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an Argentine trust fund, or fideicomiso? It is a pot of public money fed by a specific tax and reserved by law for one job. Examples include repairing national highways or subsidising household gas bills. What exactly does the US$3 billion figure measure? It is the leftover in Argentina’s national trust funds across 2024 and 2025 — money collected under earmarked taxes but not spent on its legal purpose. It is not the whole public-works budget. Has anyone been charged with a crime? No. A criminal complaint was filed on August 10, 2026, but there is no case number, no charges and no court finding. The government says it is following the budget Congress voted. Why should an investor outside Argentina care? Because the durability of the surplus underpins the bond story. Roads and water systems that go unmaintained also raise costs later for farm, mining and energy exports.

Sources: Clarin – Trust funds under scrutiny: opposition says Economy piled up over US$3 billion; La Nacion – Government collected ARS 1.5 trillion for roads and spent barely a quarter; Telefe Cordoba – Caputo defended the works funds and denied delays in execution; Clarin – Tolosa Paz files complaint against Luis Caputo over ARS 1 trillion earmarked for road works; Infobae – Ravier backs Sturzenegger and addresses the fuel tax controversy; La Gaceta – Milei government collected ARS 1.5 trillion for road works but put over ARS 1 trillion into financial investments; LMDiario – Government retained some US$3 billion of works funds to feed the zero deficit; Agenda Salta – July closed with a bottom-line surplus after a sharp spending cut; Reporte del Valle – National government withheld funds destined for roads and water infrastructure

World.title: Who Is Moving Up — and Who Is Being Left Behind in Belize?
World.content:
Who Is Moving Up — and Who Is Being Left Behind in Belize?

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News

By Nuri Mohammad: There is a conversation that Belize needs to have, but it is a difficult one because the minute you introduce race or ethnicity into a discussion, people become uncomfortable. Somebody will accuse you of trying to divide Belizeans. Somebody else will say you are playing the race card. But sometimes we have to ask uncomfortable questions.

Over the last twenty or thirty years, I have noticed something happening in Belize. I see increasing numbers of Mestizo Belizeans occupying senior positions in government, the public service and the professions—CEOs, department heads, administrators, managers and other important decision-making positions. At the same time, I don’t see Black Creole and Garifuna Belizeans reflected at those levels to the degree I remember from an earlier Belize. Maybe my observation is wrong. If it is, the statistics should prove me wrong. But if it is right, then we need to understand what happened, and I don’t believe the answer is simply racism.

We must begin with demographics. The dramatic growth of Belize’s Mestizo population did not occur only because the old Spanish-speaking Belizean communities of Corozal and Orange Walk suddenly began having exponentially more children. Belize experienced substantial migration from Central America, particularly beginning with the political upheavals and wars of the region during the late twentieth century. Thousands of people came from El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and elsewhere. They settled, raised families, became Belizeans and changed the demographic composition of the country.

At almost the same time, another demographic movement was occurring. Beginning particularly in the 1960s and continuing for decades, thousands of Creole Belizeans migrated to the United States. New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and other American cities developed significant Belizean communities. So while one population was entering Belize in considerable numbers, another population was leaving. That alone was bound to change the country.

There was a time when the Black Creole population had a significant presence in the civil service, teaching profession and other professional occupations. That was partly a product of colonial history. Creoles were concentrated in Belize City, spoke English and had relatively greater access to the educational and administrative institutions of British Honduras.

But the country changed. As Belize’s population expanded, including through immigration, the educational system had to expand with it. More schools, teachers, classrooms and government resources were required throughout the country. That was necessary, but resources are never unlimited. So here is a question we should investigate rather than assume we know the answer: as Belize expanded educational opportunities nationally, did some of the older Creole schools in Belize City deteriorate in quality and resources? And if they did, what was the consequence?

Somewhere along the road, particularly among Creole boys, we began seeing fewer young men moving successfully from primary school to secondary school, from secondary school to sixth form and from there into university and the professions. At the same time, something else was growing rapidly on the Southside of Belize City—the street.

Over the last twenty-five or thirty years, gang culture has become normalized in sections of Belize City in a way that would have been unimaginable in an earlier period. The Southside became associated nationally with gangs, shootings, poverty, dysfunctional families and crime. Eventually “Southside” stopped being simply a geographical description. It became a social label, and labels have consequences.

A young man can walk into an interview carrying more than his résumé. He carries his address, his accent, the school he attended and the neighborhood he comes from. Sometimes he carries his complexion. Nobody has to tell him, “We don’t hire Black boys from Southside.” Prejudice rarely announces itself that clearly. Instead, words like professional, reliable, presentable, articulate, stable and qualified can sometimes carry assumptions that we don’t even realize we have.

A young person from a poor neighborhood can therefore enter the competition already carrying a social profile. After twenty or thirty years, the stereotype begins feeding itself. Poor educational outcomes produce fewer qualifications. Fewer qualifications produce fewer professional opportunities. Limited opportunities strengthen street culture. Street culture reinforces the stereotype, and the stereotype makes employers more reluctant to take a chance on the next young man coming from that community. The circle closes.

Maybe racism is too simple a word for what we are seeing. What we may be looking at is something much bigger—the intersection of race, ethnicity, migration, education, geography, class and opportunity.

We must not be in denial and pretend that prejudice and colorism don’t exist. They do. There are those who have actually said to Creoles, in one form or another, “You have had your turn at leadership; it is our turn now.” Those sentiments are real, and we should not be afraid to acknowledge them. Prejudice, ethnic competition and bigotry are part of this conversation. But I believe there are much bigger forces at play than prejudice and bigotry alone. Demographics, migration, education, class, geography, the breakdown of communities and changing access to opportunity may have done more to reshape Belize over the last several decades than any single prejudice could have done by itself.

We should ask a very simple Belizean question: Does the Belize at the top look anything like the Belize at the bottom?

Walk through the ministries and look at the CEOs and senior administrators. Look at the department heads. Look at banking and corporate management, statutory bodies, universities and professional institutions. Then look at who fills the lower ranks of the Police Department and BDF, who fills our classrooms as teachers, who works in the call centers and BPO industry and who occupies the lower-paying service jobs.

And don’t guess. Count.

Break the figures down by ethnicity, gender, geography and age. Then we can have an intelligent conversation.

But Black Belizeans cannot have this conversation honestly if everything is blamed upon somebody else. We also have to ask what happened inside our own communities. Why have so many Creole boys fallen behind educationally? Why did gangs become such powerful institutions of identity and belonging? What happened to the old community organizations, sporting clubs, neighborhood leadership, strong schools, apprenticeships, political education and other institutions that once helped socialize young Black men?

What has migration done to families? What happened when some of the most ambitious, educated and upwardly mobile Creole Belizeans left for America generation after generation? That is potentially a form of brain drain whose social consequences we have never adequately measured.

If one community loses a significant part of its emerging professional class through migration while another growing community is putting its children through secondary school, sixth form and university, twenty or thirty years later we should expect the occupational landscape to look different. That isn’t necessarily conspiracy. That is sociology. But sociology can eventually produce inequality just as surely as deliberate discrimination can.

The answer cannot be to resent successful Mestizo Belizeans. A young Mestizo woman who studies hard, earns her master’s degree and becomes a CEO has not stolen anything from a Creole child. Neither should Maya advancement be regarded as somebody else’s loss. Maya Belizeans themselves suffered generations of marginalization and exclusion. Garifuna Belizeans have likewise fought extraordinary battles for education, cultural survival and recognition.

The question therefore isn’t, “Why are they moving up?” The more important question is, “Why are some of us not moving up with them?”

If the answer reveals institutional barriers, then those barriers should be removed. If it reveals educational failure, then fix the schools. If it reveals discrimination, then confront the discrimination. If it reveals family breakdown, then address why families are breaking down. If it reveals migration and brain drain, then understand their consequences. And if it reveals that our assumptions were wrong, then be courageous enough to accept the evidence. But first we need the courage to look.

Independence was supposed to mean more than replacing British administrators with Belizean administrators. It was supposed to create a society in which the child from Punta Gorda, Dangriga, Orange Walk, San Ignacio, Corozal or the Southside of Belize City could develop his or her ability and participate fully in building the nation.

So perhaps we need a national opportunity audit. Who is succeeding and who is falling behind? Who enters university and who drops out? Who becomes a CEO and who becomes a police constable? Who owns businesses and who works in them? Who migrates and who goes to prison? Most importantly, at what point in the life of a Belizean child do these roads begin to separate?

Because by the time one person is sitting behind the CEO’s desk and another is standing outside guarding the building, the real story may have begun twenty-five years earlier.

That is the conversation I think Belize needs to have. Not Mestizo against Creole. Not Black against Brown. But a serious examination of whether, in this changing Belize, we have quietly created a social structure in which your ethnicity, your neighborhood, your school and your class increasingly predict how high you are likely to climb.

If that is happening, we need to know. And if it isn’t happening, the evidence should settle the question.

Either way, let us count before we quarrel.

World.title: BREAKING: John Hernandez reportedly critically injured in early-morning San Pedro shooting
World.content:
BREAKING: John Hernandez reportedly critically injured in early-morning San Pedro shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an early-morning shooting in San Pedro Town that left John Hernandez hospitalized in critical but stable condition.

Preliminary information indicates that the shooting occurred sometime between 4:00 and 4:30 a.m. on Sunday, August 16, shortly after Hernandez arrived at a residence and parked his golf cart.

Reports are that Hernandez was opening a gate when two men arrived on a motorcycle. The passenger reportedly got off the motorcycle and opened fire on Hernandez before the pair fled the area.

Sources say approximately 12 shots were fired, reportedly in rapid succession from what was described as a fully automatic pistol. Police have not yet publicly confirmed the type of weapon used.

Hernandez was reportedly struck in the upper back and leg. He was rushed for medical treatment and, as of late Sunday morning, was listed in critical but stable condition.

Hernandez’s name has also recently been before the courts. The 26-year-old is one of three San Pedro men jointly charged with one count of arson and two counts of aggravated assault in connection with a July 31, 2024 incident in the Tranquility Bay area of northern Ambergris Caye. Hernandez, Shelby Jonathan Hernandez and Hector Pop are accused of pursuing and firing at two fishermen before allegedly setting their boat on fire.

Hernandez and Pop are currently out on bail in that case. The three accused appeared in the High Court on July 22, when Justice Nigel Pilgrim informed them that their trial could not be accommodated on the remaining 2026 calendar and would have to be scheduled for 2027. The matter is due back before the court on September 16 for mention.

Police investigations into Sunday morning’s shooting continue.

World.title: Cooling and automotive under one roof: Enrique Martinez and Sons covers Belize’s two battles
World.content:
Cooling and automotive under one roof: Enrique Martinez and Sons covers Belize’s two battles

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Every Belizean household fights two daily wars: the heat inside and the roads outside. Enrique Martinez and Sons Ltd has built its business on winning both, positioning itself as the trusted source for cooling and automotive from one location on the Philip Goldson Highway.

The cooling side carries serious names. LG dual inverter units, Trane systems and Chigo air conditioners cover everything from a single bedroom split to whole-building comfort, brands built for tropical duty and backed by a supplier that has served Belize City for years.

The automotive side is equally stocked. Linglong tires, including all-terrain Crosswind fitments for Belizean roads, sit alongside CAM2 ProMax motor oils and Premium Guard filters, with wheel alignment now offered on site, making the location a genuine one-stop for vehicle upkeep.

The store operates Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to noon and 1:00 to 5:00 p.m., and Saturdays 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., at 2 Miles Philip Goldson Highway, Belize City. Call 223-0490, WhatsApp 606-4154, or browse www.enriquemart.bz.

Cool house, healthy vehicle, one stop.

World.title: The four Bedran sisters: the women behind San Ignacio Resort Hotel’s 50 years
World.content:
The four Bedran sisters: the women behind San Ignacio Resort Hotel’s 50 years

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): As San Ignacio Resort Hotel marks its 50th anniversary, the property is honouring the family that has kept the founder’s dream alive, and in particular, the four sisters who took the reins and never let go.

Behind every great legacy are those who carry it forward, the hotel wrote in its tribute, noting that for nearly five decades the Bedran family has remained at the heart of the hotel’s story.

That story begins with Escandar Bedran and his wife, who married in September 1953 and raised seven children: Mrs. Terry B. Carter, Mrs. Nazle B. Kuylen, Mrs. Mariam B. Roberson, Mr. Abdala Bedran, Mr. Escandar Bedran, Amin Bedran and Mrs. Paulita B. Figueroa. When the patriarch, who built the hotel in 1976 after fires twice destroyed his beloved Stork Club, retired in 1996, management passed to his daughters, with his encouragement to continue the legacy of what he built.

They have done exactly that. Under the family’s stewardship, the hilltop property grew into the destination known today as the only jungle in town, keeping a Belizean family name over the door through five decades when so many local institutions changed hands or disappeared.

Fifty years on, the Bedran crest still flies over the hotel, and the founder’s daughters still carry the dream forward.

World.title: Caleigh-Rose West crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026
World.content:
Caleigh-Rose West crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize has a new queen. Caleigh-Rose West was crowned Miss Universe Belize 2026, the organization announced, declaring “the crown is yours” and wishing her an unforgettable journey as she prepares to represent Belize on the Miss Universe stage.

West emerged the official winner from the field of delegates at the national pageant, earning the right to carry Belize’s flag into one of the most watched competitions on the planet.

Her crowning night, however, did not pass without controversy. During a segment showcasing Belizean heritage, the stage’s digital backdrop displayed what viewers immediately identified as Tikal, the famous temple site located in Guatemala, rather than any of Belize’s own celebrated sites such as Xunantunich, Caracol or Altun Ha. The image spread quickly on social media, with critics calling it a glaring error for a national pageant and raising questions about oversight under the organization’s foreign ownership. The production decision was no fault of the delegates, and the organization had not publicly addressed the matter up to news time.

None of it diminishes West’s achievement. The new titleholder now begins the preparation road to the Miss Universe stage, where Belize’s queens have steadily raised the country’s profile.

Congratulations pour in for Caleigh-Rose West, Miss Universe Belize 2026.

World.title: Belize joins regional push to connect Central America’s trade and borders
World.content:
Belize joins regional push to connect Central America’s trade and borders

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize has taken a seat in the room where Central America’s future trade routes are being drawn. A delegation comprising Mrs. Narda Garcia, Chief Executive Officer in the Office of the Prime Minister, Investment and Civil Aviation, in her capacity as Alternate Governor to the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ms. Cinnamon Bottaro, Belize’s Representative on the IDB Board of Directors, participated in the Ministerial Dialogue “Central America at the Center: Connectivity and Integration for a more Competitive Region” in Panama City on August 12.

The gathering, part of the IDB’s América en el Centro initiative covering Central America, Panama and the Dominican Republic, brought together ministers of finance, transport and trade to work on practical solutions: improving regional roads and border crossings, modernizing customs and logistics, mobilizing investment and easing the movement of goods.

Discussions included Cargo Pass, an initiative to move cargo across borders safely, efficiently and with greater traceability, exactly the kind of system that will determine how quickly and cheaply Belizean exports reach regional markets.

Government says Belize’s participation ensures the country is part of the planning from the outset, because the infrastructure and trade systems designed today will shape regional commerce for decades. As the only nation holding membership in both SICA and CARICOM, Belize sees an opportunity not simply to connect with its neighbours, but to help connect Central America with Mexico and the Caribbean.

World.title: New flights, quiet season, free night: the case for Las Terrazas this fall
World.content:
New flights, quiet season, free night: the case for Las Terrazas this fall

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s fall travel season is arriving with unusual momentum, and Las Terrazas Resort and Residences on Ambergris Caye sits squarely in its path.

The momentum starts in the sky. BermudAir is launching seasonal nonstop flights to Belize City from five US airports, Boston, Raleigh-Durham, Fort Lauderdale, Orlando-Sanford and Tampa Bay’s St. Petersburg-Clearwater, with fares from US$164 and the Fort Lauderdale route beginning October 26, right as fall settles in. The airline says these will be the only nonstops from all five cities, cutting layovers out of the Belize trip for whole new markets.

On the ground, fall remains the connoisseur’s season: calmer beaches, easier tables, softer rates, and a reef every bit as brilliant as in the winter crush. Las Terrazas, the beachfront member of the L.V.X Collection of Preferred Hotels and Resorts north of San Pedro, pairs that quiet with oceanfront residences, dining, a spa and the reef at its dock.

The final piece is the math: the resort’s stay four nights, get the fifth free offer runs through December 15, stretching every fall booking an extra day.

New routes in the air, an island exhaling below, and a free night waiting. Bookings at www.lasterrazasresort.com or via WhatsApp through the Las Terrazas Resort and Residences Facebook page.

World.title: Leader of the Opposition hails people power after Speednet deal is stopped
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition hails people power after Speednet deal is stopped

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Leader of the Opposition Tracy Taegar Panton has issued a Sunday message celebrating what she calls a strong wave of civic engagement across the nation, days after Cabinet withdrew support for BTL’s proposed acquisition of Speednet.

“Your voice matters. Speaking truth to power matters. How our country is governed matters,” the Albert area representative wrote, giving thanks for “every Belizean who has risked so much to speak out, stand up, and to actively champion a more productive Belize.”

Panton’s honour roll named the coalition that stood against the deal: the BCCI, the NTUCB and its Governing Council, the NGOs, NEAB, the Council of Churches, members of the independent media, “our great United Democratic Party,” and every citizen who raised concerns on social media or peacefully protested. “We See You. We Hear You. We Appreciate You,” she wrote.

The opposition leader then turned the moment forward. “Corruption and the abuse of public office remain serious concerns,” she charged, calling on Belizeans to remain informed, vigilant and engaged, and to press for transparency, accountability and good governance “until those responsible are held to account.”

“We should never underestimate the power of an engaged citizenry,” Panton wrote. “We maintain that power belongs in the hands of the people.”

The message closed with Sunday blessings for the nation, signed One Love.

World.title: Defend truth, liberty
World.content:
Reverend Astor Carlyle (right) shakes hands with Governor General Sir Patrick Allen as Lady Allen (second right) and Chief of Defence Staff Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss Gorman (left) look on at the end of Sunday’s church service commemorating 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension, Up Park Camp in St Andrew. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Jamaicans have been urged to summon the courage of a previous generation and stand firm in defence of truth and liberty just as men and women from this region answered the call to serve when World War II plunged the world into geopolitical turmoil and economic uncertainty.



Reverend Captain Astor Carlyle made the appeal on Sunday in his sermon during the service celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Royal Air Forces Association (RAFA) Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension inside the Jamaica Defence Force’s Up Park Camp headquarters in St Andrew.

According to RAFA, the service, held under the theme ‘80 years of service, sacrifice, and unity’, marks the commencement of a year of celebrations to mark its founding.

Referencing the first lesson — Isaiah 6:1-8, which tells of the prophet Isaiah seeing a vision of God, realising he is sinful, gets cleansed by a burning coal, and volunteers to serve God by saying, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ — Rev Carlyle said that in the time of Isaiah, Judah needed someone to shoulder the responsibility of being God’s representative during great confusion.

“Throughout the Bible, God asks questions, but there is one question from the lips of God that is very relevant for a day like this when we celebrate 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association; it is a question that we heard in the first scripture reading today: Whom shall I send? Who will go for us? And this was a question asked of the prophet Isaiah in a time that needed a Godly voice and a Godly presence to bring calm and consciousness to a nation in crisis,” Carlyle told the congregation of mostly ex-servicemen and women.

“This was a time of chaos, a time of complexity, a time of corruption, and when the young Isaiah stood in the presence of God and considered the grave need, he responded with five words, ‘Here am I, send me.’ Isaiah saw what was at stake, and without concern for himself, he answered in the affirmative,” Carlyle said.

“This is a picture of the kind of spirit with which our Caribbean service members engaged the desperate call from the allied forces in 1939. It was a time of geopolitical and economic instability. Dictators were emerging in Europe and Asia, threatening the fragile peace that the Treaty of Versailles sought to ensure. The Great Depression and the subsequent invasion of Poland required the allied forces to sound the rallying call, and with a spirit of duty and a sense of mission our Caribbean servicemen said ‘Here am I, send me.’ Some trained as pilots, some trained as navigators, some were ground crew under the British Commonwealth air training plan.

“They served in Europe, they served in North Africa, they served in the Mediterranean, they served in Asia. Many Jamaicans served with the Royal Air Force bomber command and fighter command, defending Britain during air raids and helping push back the Axis forces. These young men of the Caribbean faced grave danger, but not for fame or reward, they believed in freedom that was worth defending and they paid the ultimate sacrifice. That is why we celebrate their gallantry today,” Carlyle said.

He stated that the service Jamaicans gave during the war stands as a reminder that the call to duty is for the willing, and encouraged citizens to demonstrate a willingness to serve, just as the war veterans did.

“Isaiah displayed that spirit when God asked ‘Whom shall I send?’ He didn’t give excuses, he didn’t say I am not qualified enough or I have too many responsibilities, or I am too young or I am too old. He simply said, ‘Here I am, send me.’ That is the heart of a willing servant. God expects the same of you and me, He’s asking us that same question today. As our world shows signs of economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainty God is asking who is willing, who will stand for truth, who will serve?” Carlyle told the congregation.

Earlier, in her welcome, RAFA President Major (Retired) Johanna Lewin shared that the founding members of the organisation, formed on August 16, 1946, were a band of merry men who served in the Royal Air Force during World Ward II and did so with a deep sense of pride.

RAFA, she said, initially was for those who served in the war and returned home to Jamaica “to continue their camaraderie and visit the proverbial river — the bar”.

“They wanted to ensure that all was not forgotten and that the comradeship and shared sense of duty that they developed during the war years were persevered. How many of you are familiar with Colonel Reggie Chin, who was commanding officer of the Third Battalion for many years and who served with RAF during the war? How many of you are familiar with Michael Manley, former [Jamaica] prime minister, who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during World War II? We could be here all day. It’s a long story and cannot be given justice here,” Lewin said.

She shared that RAFA started under a hut at one end of the airfield at the JDF Air Wing in Up Park Camp.

“We were offered three prime camp locations, but the one selected was what we know as Curphey Place in Swallowfield, the home of RAFA and the Jamaica Legion. The land was eventually given in perpetuity for the benefit of veterans. RAFA evolved and became more than just a means for these sassy World War II veterans to visit the ever-present river and chat and reminisce and sing about their experiences in Britain,” Lewin said.

“One of the early and major philanthropic works took place when the British charity… established Cheshire Homes, what we would term a hospice. RAFA was the first local entity to pledge $10,000, a tidy sum in those days, to build one of the units. Cheshire Homes is what we now know as the Mona Rehab. We were able to fund the original columbarium in Briggs Park and now the extension. RAFA has continued its tradition of raising funds and giving,” Lewin said.

World.title: Ahhh Ras Natango rules the world
World.content:
Tamika Williams (left) with her husband Ian (centre) and their adult son, Ayale in an undated photo. The family are the owners and operators of Ahhh Ras Natango Gallery and Garden in St James.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Tamika Williams was moved to tears on learning that her family-run Ahhh Ras Natango Gallery and Garden in St James has been ranked the world’s top attraction by travellers in an AAA Club Alliance analysis of TripAdvisor reviews.

“For Jamaica to make that list, and when you look at the calibre of countries and the calibre of attractions, and then this being a small business, a community tourism business, it just floored me. Never expected it,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

The ranking, published in July by AAA Club Alliance, was based on an analysis by ChicksX of TripAdvisor reviews, examining the frequency of positive and negative keywords visitors consistently described as “memorable”, “breathtaking”, and “better than expected”.

AAA Club Alliance explained that the study distinguished these attractions from those more commonly characterised as overrated.

Ahhh Ras Natango was ranked ahead of more well-known attractions, including the Irish National Stud & Gardens in Ireland; Al Noor Island in the United Arab Emirates; Canada’s Cabot Trail, Stone Hall Castle, and Capilano Suspension Bridge; Florida’s Stetson Mansion; Kiambethu Tea Farm in Kenya; Australia’s New Castle Memorial Walk and SkyPoint Climb; and The Rooms in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Williams said that when she received news of the results, “Mi just cry, just sat down and cry”.

That emotion was fuelled by her appreciation for the recognition, given that the attraction is still recovering from the ravages of Hurricane Melissa which devastated sections of Jamaica last October.

Four buildings, including gazebos, a restroom, and meeting area, were destroyed. The kitchen and the work area used by her husband, Ian — an artist known professionally as Ras Natango — remain out of operation, while much of the vegetation was badly damaged.

“We are operational, but we’re not fully open. We’re doing our best. We are staying the course and trying to figure out where to go, and then just out of nowhere, this came in,” Williams told the

Observer.

She described the international recognition as “an adrenaline shot” that renewed her determination to rebuild.

“I said, ‘No man, you can’t give up. No, don’t give up,’ ” she related.

Williams hopes the exposure will bring more visitors, increase awareness, and help the family restore the property. She also hopes the story will encourage others facing adversity to persevere.

“Just keep on doing what you love, because people on the outside are watching,” she said.

Opened in 2008, Ahhh Ras Natango has built its reputation largely on visitor reviews and word of mouth recommendation. Williams said the attraction has consistently held the number one position on TripAdvisor’s things to do list in Montego Bay.

She believes the attraction’s appeal lies in its story and its connection to Jamaican culture.

Williams, Ian, and their adult son, Ayale, are equal owners and have managed the business largely on their own through the COVID-19 pandemic, Hurricane Beryl in 2024, and now Hurricane Melissa.

Williams attributes their success to passion and an uncompromising commitment to every visitor.

“Our athletes do well in everything, whether it is football, whether it is especially athletics. There is a hunger in our belly when people feel marginalised and they have a dream,” she said.

“When they go on the track they leave everything there. So when every guest comes through our gate, we leave everything there,” she added.

That personal connection, she said, often leaves visitors feeling they have experienced more than a conventional tourist attraction.

“Every single guest that leaves here…they hug us up and say, ‘I feel like I just went home to my family. I feel like I had a family meeting’,” Williams told the

Observer.

Located about 2,000 feet above sea level in Camrose, the property offers panoramic views from Montego Bay towards Falmouth. Its botanical garden was created by terracing a solid rock cliff and includes an art gallery and gift shop featuring Jamaican art as well as products made on the property.

“It’s just an experience. That is what it is. It is not an attraction, it is an experience,” Williams said.

Visitors typically spend about two hours exploring the garden while learning about Jamaica’s history, culture, music, flora, and fauna.

The property is also a community resource, supporting school field trips and community activities. Williams said Camrose has also been developed as an international City of Peace.

Ecotourism remains central to the operation, with composting, rainwater harvesting, terracing, and conservation incorporated into the property.

Birds have become an even more important part of the experience since Melissa destroyed much of the vegetation. With many fruit- and seed-producing trees gone, the family has begun supplementing food for hummingbirds and other species.

“We realised that even though all the trees were gone, and the birds eat fruits and seeds, and there are no fruits and seeds, we had to supplement feeding them,” she said.

The family expects it could take five to 10 years for the larger trees to return, but Williams insists the garden remains alive.

For her, the international ranking is more than an accolade.

“It is a way for me to remember that even in the darkest hour there is light,” she said.

“…the most beautiful sunrises and sunsets is just that moment before darkness gives way to light,” Williams said.

World.title: Nine PEP stars awarded by Holness
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (fifth left) shares lens with awardees during the annual Primary Exit Profile awards function for children of employees at the Office of the Prime Minister and the Office of the Cabinet last Thursday. The awardees are (from left) Zachary Kentish, Aaron Hamilton, Jade Stewart, Kamoya McCalla, Hannah Blake, Dejaea Wright, and Amilia Davis. Two awardees, Robyn Samuels and James Seaton, are absent. Photo: JIS

NINE children of employees at the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) and the Office of the Cabinet were last Thursday recognised for successfully completing the 2026 Primary Exit Profile (PEP) examinations.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness presented the awards at OPM during the PEP annual awards function.

Holness congratulated the awardees — Hannah Blake, Amilia Davis, Aaron Hamilton, Zachary Kentish, Kamoya McCalla, Robyn Samuels, James Seaton, Jade Stewart, and Dejaea Wright — and urged them to continuously pursue knowledge.

“See learning as an exciting and a fun activity. When you get knowledge you are better off than you were without knowledge. You should always be pursuing knowledge just for the pursuit of it” Holness told the students.

He also encouraged them to have a healthy curiosity, be inquisitive, and ask questions.

“Knowledge makes you a better person, knowledge makes you a happier person, and more importantly, use the knowledge that you gain for the betterment of yourself, your family, and your country,” added Holness.

Zachary, who will be attending Ardenne High School, delivered the reply on behalf of the awardees.

He shared that the three years of preparing for PEP were not easy.

“We were tested, we endured, we were challenged and at times we felt stressed and, indeed, tired. We are grateful that we never journeyed alone. Our parents, guardians, family members, teachers, classmates, and the wider school community rallied around us every step of the way,” Zachary said.

He added that the support gave them strength, inspired hope, and reminded them to believe that they could overcome every challenge.

“We know the high school journey will come with its own set of challenges but we are assured that with you by our side and with God as guide, there is so much more we will achieve. From the PEP awardees of 2026, a big thank you,” Zachary stated.

— JIS

World.title: Hayden Panettiere, known for ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville’, dies at 36
World.content:
US actress Hayden Panettiere arrives for the world premiere of "Scream VI" at AMC Lincoln Square in New York City on March 6, 2023. (Photo by ANGELA WEISS / AFP)

Actress Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in Heroes and Nashville, has died at the age of 36, according to US media.

Her father, Skip Panettiere, confirmed her death in a statement to ABC News saying, “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

The family has requested privacy. Details surrounding the circumstances of her death were not immediately released.

Panettiere began her career as a child actress and went on to become a familiar face in television and film. She gained international recognition as Claire Bennet on the hit NBC series Heroes and later starred as Juliette Barnes in the musical drama series Nashville.

She is also known for her roles in Remember the Titans, Raising Helen, Ice Princess, and Scream 4.

Panettiere’s death comes just days before her 37th birthday, which she would have celebrated on Friday.

World.title: Franno’s last lap
World.content:
Paul Francis (left) prepares to take the urn with the cremains of his brother, legendary Jamaican track and field coach Stephen Francis, down the red-carpeted track as Sport Minister Olivia “Babsy” Grange (right) and Olympian Asafa Powell (second right) stand with athletes forming a guard of honour at the end of the thanksgiving service for Stephen Francis’s life at National Indoor Sports Centre in St Andrew on Saturday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)Photo: Garfield Robinson

HE spent a lifetime on the sidelines, stopwatch and clipboard in hand, watching athletes take their places on the track, but at the thanksgiving service for his life on Saturday, Vincent Stephen “Franno” Francis was in the spotlight. He made his final lap down a red-carpeted track, his cremains carried in a platinum urn as athletes he had trained and mentored formed a guard of honour — a fitting tribute for the legendary Jamaican track and field coach who produced world beaters.

The emotion was unmistakable as athletes fought back tears while ushering Francis out of the National Indoor Sports Centre, a stone’s throw from the National Stadium where many of them had delivered some of their greatest performances. This time, however, there was no race to prepare for, no stopwatch to start, and no final instructions to give, only the painful realisation that they were saying goodbye to the coach who had spent a lifetime helping them find their way to the finish line, and now they were returning the favour.

For approximately five minutes, sprint legends Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, Shericka Jackson, Kishane Thompson, Elaine Thompson Herah, and many more who spent years being taught the art and science of sprinting stood still as family members, friends, Government officials, and colleagues looked on, reminiscing on the life of a world-class coach.

A nod to his alma mater, Wolmer’s Boys’ School, the sports centre and many attendees were decked in maroon and gold for the four-hour-long service that was enveloped in an atmosphere that swung from grief to celebration.

Pot covers echoed during tributes about Francis’s excellent track record, tears flowed when travelling down memory lane, laughter filled the room at comical moments, and musical tributes and selections provided much-needed comfort.

In his tribute, delivered by Finance Minister Fayval Williams, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness praised Francis for demonstrating what was possible when natural talent was matched with world-class coaching, structure, and preparation. He noted that, through the formation of the Maximising Velocity and Power (MVP) Track Club, Francis helped create a pathway for Jamaican athletes to develop at home, at a time when many were leaving the island in search of training opportunities abroad.

“Athletes under his guidance became Olympic and World champions, record holders and household names. Yet his influence cannot be measured by counting medals alone. He developed people, he established standards, and he challenged athletes to become more disciplined, more prepared, and more demanding of themselves,” wrote Holness.

“He also helped prove that a Jamaican coaching programme could consistently produce performances of the highest international standard. In that sense, his impact reached well beyond MVP. He contributed to the evolution of the Jamaican coaching profession and to a stronger national system of athlete development,” he said.

It was for these reasons that Sports Minister Olivia Grange urged the congregation not to mourn, but to celebrate the man who possessed an extraordinary vision backed by purpose and confidence that what he was doing would bring the results that he envisioned.

“Francis understood that talent was only the beginning. Talent had to be developed, potential had to be channelled, and dreams had to be matched by commitment. That philosophy, my brothers and sisters, helped to shape athletes and contributed significantly to Jamaica’s remarkable place in world athletics. Francis possessed technical mastery. He studied speed like a scientist. Above all, he had a strong belief in Jamaica and the potential of our people,” said Grange.

She added that to honour his legacy, the Government is in discussions to provide student-athletes at the University of Technology, Jamaica, the home of the MVP track club, a scholarship in his name.

The move was welcomed by president of the university Dr Kevin Brown, who thanked Francis for choosing the campus as his training ground and placing the institution on the map, one athlete at a time. He remembered Francis for his bluntness, discipline, and belief in the potential of Jamaica, joking that he never wasted words and advocated fiercely for his athletes.

An emotional Brigitte Foster-Hylton and Asafa Powell, two sprint legends who reaped the rewards of Francis’s brilliance, stood as living evidence of his legacy, though struggling to steady their voices as they fought back tears. Between the emotion, they recalled cherished memories, from dodging train conductors in Italy to travelling in Francis’s old car, thanking the coach who had taken a chance on them, believed in their potential, and pushed them towards global success.

“Everything I became started with one man who saw something in a young man before anyone else did,” said Powell, Foster-Hylton finishing his speech as he broke down in tears.

She thanked Francis for every lesson, sacrifice, laugh, and opportunity, noting that he did not just change her life, he changed countless lives.

“Rest well, Franno. Your whistle might be silent, but your legacy lives on,” she said through tears.

Eulogised by his brother, Paul, who also spoke through shaky breaths, the decorated coach was remembered as a friend, a loyalist, a protector of his athletes, a family man, and a coach.

Adrian Laidlaw wiped away tears as he declared that delivering a tribute to his best friend was the hardest job he was ever tasked with. He said when Francis closed his eyes on July 4, 2026, a piece of Jamaica left with him, and his legacy will always be remembered.

Recounting cherished memories of a man he described as both mentor and friend, MVP President Bruce James said Francis made countless sacrifices in his mission to put Jamaica firmly on the international athletics stage, remaining committed to the vision even in the face of doubt.

James recalled that Francis’s dedication to his athletes never wavered, even from his hospital bed, where he continued asking for updates on their progress — a final testament to a coach whose commitment to his craft and athletes endured to the very end.

“History has proven you right, Franno. The World records, the Olympic records, the World champions, the Olympic champions, the world athletes of the year, the numerous athletes who won medals on the global stage achieved more than they ever thought possible and became better versions of themselves because they were a part of MVP,” said James in a written tribute.

World.title: KFC eats into jerk sales
World.content:
Morant Bay jerk pork vendor Johnny sharing his experience since KFC set up shop in the St Thomas capital town late last year. He told the Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”. Now he prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

TRADITIONAL jerk vendors in Morant Bay, St Thomas, are reporting a decline in their business since fast food giant KFC officially opened its historic first restaurant in the parish in January this year.

But the vendors say while sales are down they are not being squeezed out of the business which, for years, has attracted residents of the parish as well as scores of people passing through the town.

One jerk pork vendor, who gave his name only as Johnny, last Thursday told the Jamaica Observer that while his business remains open, “it’s not as warm as it once was”.

Johnny, who also works as a butcher, said the business has slowed down and the increase in sales he normally sees during holiday periods did not materialise this year.

He told the Sunday Observer that before KFC opened its doors he would prepare some 30 pounds of pork each day and most times it would “sell out”.

According to Johnny, he now prepares about 20 pounds of pork daily and even that amount is not always completely sold.

He pointed out that even his children sometimes ask for chicken from KFC.

“So I have to go in there and spend to buy what they want,” said Johnny, who added that he continues to receive support from loyal customers who prefer his jerked pork.

Another jerk vendor, who requested anonymity, said the arrival of KFC would naturally result in some loss of business for local food operators, but he does not believe it poses a major threat.

“I don’t know, it would be a downgrade in a sense because most people gravitate towards the KFC and dem business deh,” the vendor said as he told the Sunday Observer that there had been “a slight drop-off” in his business since KFC opened.

“It’s gradually going down, but sometimes it’s up again,” the vendor said, even as he underscored that he welcomes the presence of the immensely popular KFC.

He pointed to the demand for employment opportunities and development in the parish, and described KFC’s arrival as a positive development for the integrated industrial and commercial complex dubbed the Morant Bay Urban Centre.

“People need jobs as well, so I would say it’s a good thing,” the vendor said.

KFC invested $350 million to establish its Morant Bay restaurant which provides jobs for more than 50 people.

The store was warmly received by several residents of St Thomas with one person describing the opening as “a wonderful and historic moment for the parish”.

At the official opening in January, Mark Myers, managing director of Restaurants of Jamaica — the operators of the KFC franchise locally — said the decision to locate in Morant Bay was deliberate and rooted in confidence in the area’s potential.

“This opening is about more than adding another restaurant to the network. It reflects a deliberate decision to invest in communities beyond Kingston and to grow in places where opportunity and potential continue to emerge.

“When plans for the Morant Bay Urban Centre were first taking shape we saw an opportunity to be part of something transformational. We want to participate in the continued development of this parish, to invest early and to grow alongside the community — [and] that conviction is what brought us here,” Myers said then.

World.title: Vision. Mission. Spirit. Impact
World.content:
Djimon Hounsou.

The fourth annual Screenwriters’ Workshop hosted by Strike Star Entertainment is set to take place over two days from September 15-16 at Edna Manley College of the Visual and Performing Arts.

The workshop, which is designed to introduce young and aspiring professionals to the film industry, will feature a keynote address by respected American film director Benny Boom.

Other presenters and panellists include Vanessa Ballesteros (television producer and showrunner); actor John Chambers; producer, writer and executive Marvin Peart; Soyini Chang, entrepreneur, strategist, and creative executive; Morris Sinclair, cultural entrepreneur and project strategist; screenwriter Tyrone Rashard; John Buffalo Mailer, producer, screenwriter, journalist and playwright; Bryce Wilson, formerly of the music duo Groove Theory and a creative director, actor and producer; actor Djimon Hounsou; editor Olivia Rutigliano; and Cess Silvera, director, producer and screenwriter.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Ricky Lee, CEO and founder of Strike Star Entertainment, explained why he decided to host the screenwriter workshop in Jamaica.

“I’ve always believed Jamaica has one of the richest storytelling cultures in the world. The creative energy here is raw, honest, and deeply rooted in lived experience. When Paul Eckstein [American actor, television writer and producer] passed, I felt an even stronger pull to continue the work he inspired — creating spaces where emerging writers can grow, be seen, and be supported. Edna Manley College represents that same spirit of artistic discipline and cultural pride. Hosting the workshop here allows us to honour Paul’s legacy while investing directly in Jamaica’s next generation of storytellers,” said Lee.

The very first workshop was held at The Mico University College, which Lee shared was a deeply meaningful beginning.

“Our partner Steven Golding teaches at Mico, and he helped connect us to the institution. Mico is one of Jamaica’s first teachers’ colleges, so starting there felt aligned with Paul’s belief in education, access, and community. That foundation continues to guide everything we do,” explained Lee.

He told the Observer that the objective behind the workshop is to expand creative minds and opportunities.

“Over two days, participants learn the fundamentals of screenwriting, story structure, character development, and the business of film. We focus on mentorship, industry exposure, and building confidence; the same values Paul championed throughout his career. We’re targeting emerging and aspiring screenwriters — young creatives, students, and anyone who feels called to write for film or television. You don’t need industry experience; you just need imagination, commitment, and a desire to grow,” said Lee.

Interested participants can visit Strike Star Entertainment online and register.

“Jamaica has extraordinary talent,” opined Lee, “what’s often missing is access, mentorship, and industry level exposure… By bringing global professionals directly to Jamaican creatives we’re strengthening the foundation of the country’s emerging film ecosystem. And in many ways, we’re continuing the work Paul believed in: Empowering storytellers and expanding opportunity,” he said.

Benny Boom, who directed the music video for Sean Paul’s Like Glue as well as videos for several acts, including Busta Rhymes, Nas, Nelly, LL Cool J, Nicki Minaj, Akon, 50 Cent, and GloRilla, is best known for directing the 2017 Tupak Shakur biopic All Eyez on Me.

He told the Observer what participants attending the workshop can expect.

“I’m bringing my experience, my perspective, and my commitment to helping writers understand how powerful their voice is. Paul Eckstein was someone I deeply respected; not just for his creativity, but for the way he championed storytellers. His belief in developing writers and expanding access is something I carry with me. So, when I step into this workshop, I’m bringing that same spirit — honesty, mentorship, and a real desire to help emerging writers elevate their craft,” said Benny Boom. “You can expect clarity and real, practical guidance. I want writers to understand how directors read scripts, how we translate words into images, and what makes a story visually compelling. I want participants to walk away with tools they can use immediately.”

According to Benny Boom, he couldn’t turn down the offer to be a part of the workshop.

“I said yes right away. Ricky shared the vision, and he shared Paul’s influence on this workshop. Paul was someone whose work and creative energy I admired, so being part of something inspired by him felt meaningful. Coming back for a second year was an easy decision, this workshop is doing real work for Jamaican creatives, and I’m proud to support it,” said the respected director.

World.title: Fears flow in St Thomas
World.content:
Resident Charline Gabas stands in front her home and points to the dirt pushed along the edge of the path where the Plantain Garden River flows in Bath, St Thomas, last Thursday.Photos: Karl Mclarty

JUST over nine months after Hurricane Melissa sent residents of Bath, St Thomas, scrambling from their houses as the Plantain Garden River tore into its banks, washed away a parked car, and threatened to swallow lands inches from their homes, residents say a recent riverbank intervention has done little to ease their fears.

Dirt pushed along the edge in July has provided some protection, residents acknowledge, but they insist it is no substitute for a groyne in and the proper channelling of the river.

Therefore, they are warning that another bout of heavy rain could once again send floodwaters towards their homes, further eroding the riverbank and putting the wider community, including Bath Primary School, at risk.

They are also adamant that another major weather event, similar to Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the island on October 28, 2025, could finally cause their homes to collapse into the river’s path.

When the Jamaica Observer returned to the area last Thursday the scene was markedly different from the one residents had confronted during Melissa’s onslaught last year.

Dirt had been pushed along the edge of the area where the riverbank had broken away, while additional dirt had been placed in the space through which the river flows, apparently to obstruct the water’s path and keep it from pushing towards the vulnerable section.

But for residents who have spent years watching the river steadily eat away at the landscape, the intervention has brought only limited reassurance.

Charline Gabas, who lives in the community at the very edge, acknowledged that the dirt has made the immediate area feel somewhat safer, but said it has not addressed what she considers the fundamental problem — the absence of a proper channel to carry the river away from the homes.

“Don’t get me wrong, enuh, if this was not here I would not be able to stand up here, cause when mi stand up here suh it is a little bit safer. But listen, what we are saying — because we have been here for years — they need to take out that piece and channel it to that dry piece of land over the other side, dig it and carry down there suh so [that] when the river comes down it goes that side and follows that channel instead of come over here. Because with how it stay now, the water is going to come over her same way,” Gabas told the Jamaica Observer.

Last October, as Hurricane Melissa battered Jamaica, sections of the Plantain Garden River bank collapsed, prompting residents living nearby to quickly evacuate their homes. Video footage circulated on social media showed residents fleeing as a section of the riverbank gave way, sweeping away a parked car in the process.

For residents, the episode was not entirely unexpected.

During an October visit, Bath resident Theodore Bailey said the community had been calling for the river to be properly protected for more than two decades. He pointed to cracks in the soil near the threatened homes and warned that the saturated ground could still give way even after the hurricane had passed.

Furthermore, the river’s movement has also changed the landscape over time, according to Gabas who rejected the suggestion that residents had simply built their homes too close to the river’s path.

She said the river was once much farther from the houses and that the encroachment had occurred gradually, as the water continued to wash away the land.

“We could not see river and build we house beside it, we are not that stupid… That is what I am trying to tell people, that the river was all the way over there suh but over time it keep on coming over and washing away the land,” she said, noting that she has lived in the community for 19 years and has watched the river steadily encroach on the land.

Initially, residents had suggested that large boulders be used to strengthen the vulnerable section, similar to measures they had seen elsewhere.

But Gabas said the current deterioration of the riverbank means that approach is no longer enough.

“At the time we ask them fi turn the river and we did a seh get the big stone dem, at that time it never suh bad suh we did a suggest they could use the boulders like wah dem use over Yallahs or Port Royal road [Palisadoes]. But then it get so bad now so that is no longer an option. The river have to groyne back, turn the river and groyne it back,” Gabas said.

Tracy-Ann Emanuel, another Bath resident, said the current intervention does not appear capable of withstanding the force of the river during sustained rainfall. She argued that the river needs to be properly trained — a process that, in practical terms, involves controlling and directing the water’s course so that it does not continue spilling into vulnerable areas.

“Well this nuh mek any sense. They need to rebuild a groyne, this place really need fi groyne back, because if one next big shower of rain come we are going to be in problem, so when PG [Plantain Garden] river a come it a guh push back the dirt fi come over here suh,” she reasoned.

Concerns were also raised about how long it took officials to address the issue. According to Gabas, the work was carried out roughly three to four weeks before the Sunday Observer revisited the area last Thursday.

She said residents had become increasingly concerned as the hurricane season progressed and they saw no work being done yet were given no explanation about who was responsible for the eventual intervention.

She said the lack of consultation has added to the frustration.

According to Gabas, workers arrived, carried out the work, and left without explaining to residents what was being done or what the intervention was intended to achieve. At the time of the Sunday Observer’s visit she said residents did not know which agency had undertaken the work.

Gabas said residents are particularly anxious because relocating is not a realistic option for many of them.

“We cannot move, we nuh have any options. When hurricane came October and we had to move out we things because of what happened and by November I had to move in again [that was one thing], but [now] mi nuh have a next option. Mi nuh have the money to buy land and start over and make a next house again,” she said.

So residents are watching the weather closely and worrying about what another prolonged period of rainfall could bring.

Gabas said the dirt has at least created enough of a barrier to make it possible for her to stand at the edge of the vulnerable area without feeling as exposed as before. But she does not regard that as evidence that the underlying danger has been addressed.

She also pointed to what she sees as a gap between the authorities carrying out physical work and the residents living with the consequences.

Gabas said the Sunday Observer team was the first group, since Hurricane Melissa, to return and speak directly with residents about the condition of the river and their concerns.

“From Hurricane Melissa come last year October unnu a the first set of people who come and have a conversation with we and ask we about the river, nobody else. Anybody else we see, dem just come work and point; dem nuh know we and we nuh know dem. The tractor man seh a work him get fi push dirt and him just a work! The rest a people dem just come in and look, and point finger, and gwaan,” she expressed.

The National Works Agency (NWA) has since been identified as the agency responsible for the intervention work.

Stephen Shaw, the NWA’s manager of communication and customer services, confirmed to the Sunday Observer last Friday that the agency carried out the intervention but said he could not provide details at the time.

For the residents of Bath, however, the immediate concern is less about who moved the dirt and more about whether it will hold when the river next rises.

World.title: Czech PM Babiš apologizes for picking flowers in national park
World.content:
Andrej Babiš arrives at the Elysee Presidential Palace in Paris on July 13, 2026. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

“I will definitely pay a fine if necessary, of course,” he said.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš apologized Sunday for picking flowers in a protected area on Lysá hora, a mountain in eastern Czechia, saying he would pay a fine if necessary.

Babiš said in a Facebook video that he plucked the flowers while remembering a late colleague from his ANO movement with whom he had previously climbed the mountain.

“Maybe I broke some law, for which I apologize and I will definitely pay a fine if necessary, of course,” he said.

World.title: Burnham exchanged messages with impersonator of top Trump aide
World.content:
The British embassy in Washington was so concerned about the incident that it raised it with the White House, two of the officials said. Like others in this article, they were granted anonymity to discuss a matter of national security.

Inside the U.K. government, there were fears that Wiles’ phone had been hacked again. The White House declined to comment.

Last year, the White House and the FBI launched an investigation after senators, governors and U.S. business executives received texts and phone calls from someone claiming to be Trump’s chief of staff.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Wiles told associates her cellphone contacts had been hacked.

What was discussed in the exchange with Burnham — and when the messages were sent — is unclear, with the erroneous contact kept a closely-guarded secret.

Burnham became PM on July 20, but it was clear he was on course to succeed Keir Starmer from the moment he won the Makerfield by-election on June 18.

World.title: Germany rethinks law protecting politicians from insults
World.content:
Moritz Oppelt, the CDU justice minister of Germany’s southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg echoed the sentiment, arguing the law should serve only its original intent of protecting local politicians, who are often subject to particular vitriol.

“Top politicians can and must be able to withstand tough criticism,” he said. “It is fundamental to our democracy, and part of our understanding of democracy in Germany, that people are free to discuss political decisions at the federal and state levels and criticize them very harshly. That does not mean that insults in the political sphere should become normalized. There are, of course, limits.”

Variations of this view find consensus across Germany’s fractured political spectrum. The far-left Left Party and far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party want the law abolished outright, while the CDU, Greens and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) all support revising it.

“Politicians like Friedrich Merz insult ordinary people in this country every day by calling them lazy or malingerers,” said Luke Hoss, a Left lawmaker, referring to the chancellor’s remarks that Germans should work more to boost economic growth. “The provision creates a special criminal offense that applies only to politicians and should be abolished.”

Tobias Peterka, an AfD lawmaker, said tough criticism comes with the job. “Anyone who voluntarily enters politics and exercises public authority must — as Germany’s Federal Constitutional Court has repeatedly emphasized — tolerate harsher criticism than private citizens, not less,” he argued.

While a version of the law giving special protection to politicians, Section 188 of the criminal code, has existed since 1951, former Chancellor Angela Merkel’s government in 2021 strengthened the legislation as part of broader efforts to combat right-wing extremism and hate speech.

World.title: ‘Deliberate negligence’: Russian nuclear power company with EU operations accused of violating safety standards
World.content:
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Europe to impose sweeping sanctions on the country, Rosatom has tried to convince European governments that it remains a reliable and competent supplier in the nuclear power market. But the accusations of safety breaches could add to existing concerns over the Kremlin-controlled company’s operations in the EU.

In an emailed statement to POLITICO, Rosatom said it upholds the highest levels of nuclear safety and had done so throughout the construction of El Dabaa. The company declined to comment on whether it had received the letter or the complaints from Egypt's Nuclear Power Plants Authority, which did not respond to multiple requests for comment about its communications with Rosatom.

“The high standard of work organisation, the quality management system and the safety culture are affirmed by the sustained attention paid to the project by the political leadership of the Russian Federation and the Arab Republic of Egypt, as well as by the leadership of the International Atomic Energy Agency, whose representatives regularly attend key project milestones,” said the company by email, adding that a recent ceremony for one of El Dabaa’s reactor units was attended by Russian, Egyptian and IAEA officials.

Egypt's El Dabaa is located on the Mediterranean Sea coast, some 300 km northwest of Cairo. | Alexander Ryumin/TASS via Belga

None of the allegations contained in the letter, presented to Rosatom by POLITICO, have been “confirmed within the contractual, technical and oversight procedures envisaged by the project," read the company’s statement.

Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said in July he expected the construction of all four El Dabaa reactors to finish by 2030, with the first reactor unit set to begin producing power by 2028. No nuclear fuel has yet been introduced to the site. Rosatom's Egyptian plant will use the same technology at the heart of Hungary's Paks II project, the Kremlin-backed nuclear expansion that has repeatedly raised tensions between Budapest and the European Commission.

The Commission told POLITICO it was not aware of the confidential documents and allegations they contain. “For the EU, nuclear safety is a key priority,” said a Commission spokesperson.

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.
